body:
I would like to make a small change to this definition, which would help make allocators a bit more efficient. Essentially we have 3 regions of memory:
- Region A: `0..old_size` (`old_size` parameter passed into `grow`)
- Region B: `old_size..allocated_size` (`allocated_size` is the size returned by `alloc`)
- Region C: `allocated_size..new_size` (`new_size` parameter passed into `grow`)

The semantics of regions A and C are pretty clear: A is preserved, C is initialized according to `init`.

For region B, it should be *implementation defined* whether the memory is preserved or initialized according to `init`. This is mainly relevant when using `AllocInit::Zeroed`:
- As long as you haven't touched region B since the `alloc` (which is the case for `Vec`), it is guaranteed to be zeroed.
- An allocator using `mremap` can just resize the VM region directly without needing to zero partial pages. (The previous allocation will have been rounded up to page size, new pages are always zero).

True, but I think there is no reasonable way to avoid that race: we need one thread to be blocked on some I/O and another thread to cause process exit. While the first thread is blocked on I/O it cannot notify the other thread (by definition), and the second thread does not have a way of knowing the first thread is truly blocked on I/O on its own unless we are willing to check `/proc/self/task/*/stat` or something similar.

I think we can reasonably expect that the main thread does not exit before the spawned thread blocks on `accept()` in most cases.

The error is indeed misleading, because what you're suggesting isn't what the error means.

The error is trying to say that *evaluating* the constant expression may only succeed for some "values" of the generic parameter.
The missing piece of the puzzle is a way to put that expression in a `where` clause to force the caller to evaluate it, ruling out post-monomorphization errors (#68436).

Note that [expressions using generics can still evaluate](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=ba0ae8e0eb712b342a61a776ac52c62f) just fine while remaining polymorphic.

When using incremental mode combined with `--emit llvm-bc`, if the codegen unit is not cached, the bitcode will be written and the `CompiledModule` will get `bytecode` set to Some. ```bash

```bash
$ ls
a.rs
a.bc
incr/
$ rm a.bc
$ rustc -Cincremental=incr --emit llvm-bc a.rs
a.rs
incr/
$ # a.bc is missing
```

body:
> Why do we need to "move the discriminant" ?

The intuition was that *all fields* (including the discriminant) had to be sorted by the alignment for optimal (i.e. minimal) size.

The interesting thing we hadn't realized, and I just spent some time thinking through, is that this sort of situation is still optimal:
* discriminant: `u32` (`align=4`)
* fields with `align<4`, total padding `0`, `1`, `2` or `3` bytes
* fields with `align>=4`

The first group of fields can be (conceptually) swapped with the discriminant, resulting in the sorted order that we know is optimal, but there's no way the padding could change, because they can't tell apart being at the start of the type or being after the discriminant (both are aligned to a multiple of `4`).

And the second group of fields starts on an offset that's a multiple of `4`, so they're not affected by the padding inside the first group of fields.

This has implications beyond `enum`s, e.g. `(u32, u8, u32, u64)` has minimal padding (`7`) and sorting is unnecessary - in fact, I can't think of any permutation of that tuple that would be larger than `24` bytes, [and we can test that](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=5eb19ef9861e388f56bce93a762871c2).
However, I'm not sure if there's any point in doing anything clever based on that finding, outside of `enum`s.

Can you make a separate PR that removes `optimize &= align.bytes() == 1;` and adds some tests?

body:
Thanks for your PR! I have two main comments:

---

I don't quite like the second part of your error messages. The first part (stating the condition) is nice. But the second part is not explicit enough for me. For example, instead of 

> `insertion index should be <= len, got {} <= {}", index, len`

... I would write something like this:

> `insertion index should be <= len, but the insertion index is {} and len is {}", index, len`

This, of course, is not a particularly nice English as we will repeat the names (indices/len) a lot. I think clarity and explicitness in these error messages is more important than nice English, but maybe we can improve it still. How about one of these?

- ```"assertion `index <= len` failed: insertion index is {} and len is {}"```
- ```"index out of bounds: insertion index is {} and len is {}, but `index <= len` should hold"```

---

My second concern is performance. These are methods potentially called in hot loops. Panicking with a static string generates way less code than using the fmt machinery. And making those methods larger influences icache and inlining behavior, having a potentially large impact on performance. This could be (at least partially) mitigated by created special `#[cold]` functions that simply panic. In any case, I'd like to check with `@rust-timer`.

Hi there and thanks for your PR!

You are right, we should certainly improve `stream_position`. However, I don't think your changes are the way to go, for several reasons. Making sure that this new struct field is always up to date adds maintenance burden, for example. I also think the patch as is is still broken in several places (CI is not green, for example).

The easier and better solution is what @Luro02 suggested. However, as suggested, it is not correct. `self.pos` does unfortunately not refer to the position in the underlying stream, but is simply the start of the "useful" data in `buf`. The actual useful buffer is `self.buf[self.pos..self.cap]`, to be precise.

I believe we can obtain the actual stream position like this:

```rust
fn stream_positon(&mut self) -> io::Result<u64> {
    self.inner.stream_position().map(|inner_pos| inner_pos - self.buffer().len())
}
```

Hmm... I don't think we have side effects in the sense that there might be a user-defined function call or something hiding in an `Rvalue` (excluding `ConstKind::Unevaluated`). However there are somethings that might be termed side effects like:

- de-referencing a pointer
  - Removing a deref means we could potentially be removing UB if the pointer isn't actually valid. That *seems* ok to me. 

- Boxing values
  - I believe this lowers to a call to the global allocator which means you could observe this *not* happening via a custom allocator. 

- {Checked,}Binary ops could over/under flow.

In general, `Rvalues` except for these seem side-effect free to me (excluding `ConstKind::Unevaluated` and things that contain `Place` values with projections):

- `BinaryOp`
- `CheckedBinaryOp`
- `Cast`
- `NullaryOp`
- `UnaryOp`

body: That is beautiful! ❤️
author: wesleywiser

body:
`CheckedBinaryOp` doesn't have a side-effect as over/under flow will just return that it had over/under flowed. `UnaryOp` is used to implement both negation and bitwise not. The later is always side-effect free. `Cast(CatKind::Pointer(_), _, _)` is side-effect free I think, but `Cast(CastKind::Misc, _, _)` could remove a ptr-int cast or int-ptr cast. `NullaryOp(NullOp::SizeOf, ty)` only needs to ensure that `layout_of` doesn't error on the type.

> Boxing values
> 
>     * I believe this lowers to a call to the global allocator which means you could observe this _not_ happening via a custom allocator.

Yes, it lowers to the `exchange_malloc` lang item, which uses `Global.alloc`:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/dd155df0a69338757ca39a2a606a6accb7b8d342/src/liballoc/alloc.rs#L225

Removing this allocation would be equivalent to any function in liballoc or libstd changing when and how much it allocates though, so I don't think anybody can depend on it anyway.

body:
The core problem for which I cannot find an elegant solution is how to have multiple allocation ids for the same thread local static. The options I though about are:

1.  Duplicating entries of thread-local statics in [`tcx.alloc_map`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/mir/interpret/struct.AllocMap.html). However, `tcx.alloc_map` has an invariant that all statics are deduplicated and I do not think we should start violating it.
2. On the first access of a thread-local static, allocate a fresh thread specific allocation id of a "regular" memory allocation. This could be implemented in at least two ways:

    1. (The current implementation in this PR.) `canonical_alloc_id` only reserves a fresh allocation id, but does not actually allocate memory. The memory gets allocated by `get_raw` and `get_raw_mut` in the same way as for normal statics. The only caveat is that the freshly allocated id does not contain information about the original static and, therefore, we need this additional callback `resolve_maybe_global_alloc` to retrieve information about it.
   2. We could also do the actual allocation in `canonical_alloc_id` because the `memory.alloc_map` is wrapped in `RefCell`. In this way, we would not need the `resolve_maybe_global_alloc` callback. However, as far as I understand, for this to work we would need to make field `alloc_map` and function `get_global_alloc` public.

For me personally, the current implementation felt a little bit more elegant than alternatives. However, I would be happy to change to a different approach.

What is your opinion on this? @bjorn3 @RalfJung @oli-obk

body:
This seems quite roundabout... so given the lazy `AllocId` of a thread_local static (the one that resolves to a `DefId`), we first call `canonical_alloc_id` to map this *away*, to a "real" `AllocId`, and then here we have to map it *back*.

I think we should avoid that round-trip. I will think about how to do that, but input is welcome.
author: RalfJung
RalfJung

body:
The constraint comes from the stack frame [definition](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/96d77f0e5f103612d62b85938aacfb33f5768433/src/librustc_mir/interpret/eval_context.rs#L57):
```rust
pub body: &'mir mir::Body<'tcx>,
```
Since before the stack was part of the interpreter, all uses could infer this bound. Moving the stack behind the `Machine` trait requires this bound to be explicitly stated everywhere. I have not found a way to avoid this.

> Hm, why would we want the symlink approach over an environment variable read or something (at runtime, I guess, set during our tests?)

Because `rustup` places `rust-src` in a certain directory, and presumably distros can too, so we'd want to use that, and using a symlink would transparently let that work for local build sysroots, without adding an insta-stable env var.

> and we can make it optional I think, in the sense that you need it for tests to pass but if you don't have it things won't fail to build entirely.

Ah, good point, do we have a way for `src/bootstrap` to emit a warning if it tried something and that failed?
I'm thinking I would try to create the symlink, then do the same check `rustc` does (look for `src/libstd/lib.rs` inside there), and if either fails, warn instead of failing the build.

body:
Hmm, I'm not sure which is the best setup. It seems like we have 3 fairly distinct cases:

* `BuiltinCandidate { has_nested: true }` -- used for copy, clone, and `Sized`, though in slightly different ways between those traits
* `BuiltinCandidate { has_nested: false }` -- used for `Unpin` with *movable generator types* specifically
* `AutoImplCandidate` -- used for other auto traits
* `DiscriminantKind` -- for the discriminant trait we are adding now

Of these, `BuiltinCandidate { has_nested: false }` is the "odd one out", because it applies not only to a specific trait, but to a specific *self type* for that trait. Are we actually exposing "movable generators" anywhere in the language? I don't think so, and I don't know that we have any real plans to do so either, right? I wonder if we should simplify things by removing them.

Ignoring `has_nested: false` case for the moment: it seems like the main piece of code that wants to discriminate between traits is the projection code?

One option that might be nice is to have

```rust
enum CandidateKind {
    ...
    BuiltinCandidate(BuiltinCandidateKind)
}

enum BuiltinCandidateKind {
    AutoTrait,

    SizedTrait,
    CopyTrait,
    CloneTrait,

    DiscriminantKindTrait
}
```

Currently, in select.rs anyway, those built-in candidates each behave "kind of" differently, and are grouped in the  groups I showed above. But I suspect that the *select.rs* handling for all of these cases could be combined, at least if we added a limitation on auto traits that they can never have any predicates (true for all known auto traits, and at least *somewhat* required for soundness around coinduction anyhow). In each case the idea would be that you extract some set of types for the "recursive obligations" (sometimes empty, as in the case of `DiscriminantKind`).

The project.rs handling meanwhile could use these types to pick out the right case.

This leaves the question of how to handle `Unpin` -- we could certainly add a special case tothe list above, like `UnpinTraitMovableGenerator` and it would fit ok I suppose.

This seems like it might be a nice refactoring, but it also feels like the majority of this refactoring is orthogonal from this PR. But it feels like it might be nice to do beforehand. @lcnr if you're interested I could try to describe what I have in mind in more detail.

I think your current wording of your latest commit is fine.

The unsafetyness is basically because `len * mem::size_of::<T>()` is passed to `AllocRef::dealloc` when dropping the `Box`, this must be a valid call.
author: TimDiekmann

body: Yes, but I don't understand why `self.cap` vs `self.capacity()` was important, and why it is not relevant any more?
author: RalfJung

body:
> I don't understand why self.cap vs self.capacity() was important, and why it is not relevant any more?

It was only important as calls to `shrink_to_fit` have set `self.cap` in any case, even for ZSTs. Calling `into_box` then returned a boxed slice with the `boxed.len() == self.cap`. As `len` is now passed explicitly to `into_box`, `self.cap` isn't used here anymore. 

> So if I see it correctly, the difference between self.cap and self.capacity() only arises in case of mem::size_of::<T>() == 0. And in that case the size of the Box is zero anyway so it does not matter?

Yes, that's correct. When using `RawVec<ZST>`, `AllocRef` is called with a `layout.size() == 0`, and `self.capacity()` always return `usize::MAX`. Theoretically *any* length can be passed to `into_box` here. However, the safety constraint is still a little bit more conservative. For example calling `RawVec::<ZST>::with_capacity(10)` forbids calling `into_box(5)`, but this would be well defined. Personally I'd keep the safety clause as mentioned above, because then ZSTs and none-ZSTs are exchangeable.

body:
I completely agree with you. I think the precision should be more obvious. But moving these mathematical consts to associated constants were met with resistance in the RFC (😢).

The reason I went with the way I did was that:
1. `src/libcore/num/{f32,f64}.rs` had examples using this format (`to_degrees` and `to_radians`). So, consistency. Otherwise we should probably change those instances into something else also.
2. Continuing to import the `std::f32` module will shadow the constants on the type, so the constants from the module will still be used. This means:
    * it will be even harder to ever argue for a deprecation of the old constants, because it would generate warnings in all such code.
    * IDEs that automatically show docs etc would also show the docs for the module constant, which say "Use f32::EPSILON instead" which would be a bit confusing maybe.

I could do `use std::f32::consts as f32consts;` or something to avoid all problems, like you hint you would probably do yourself. But it's ugly, in the sense that the only way to use the standard library constants in a nice way is to always rename them on import. That's my main problem here. There is no way to do it nicely with the way the constants are currently exposed.

What do you think we should do?

1. Error differently for polymorphic and monomorphic constants, doing the former post-monomorphization, and the latter pre-monomorphization (inconsistent).

3. Error for neither and insert a trap in codegen, but @RalfJung [would probably be even more unhappy about that](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/67134#discussion_r355697861).

`futures::future::Pending<T>` uses `PhantomData<T>` so it's covariant (but also interacts with dropck).

`async-std` uses `pub async fn pending<T>() -> T` which means it's necessarily invariant (although the private `struct Pending<T>`, that it relies on, looks identical to the `futures` one).

Given that a value of `T` never exists at any point and the parameter only exists for trait dispatch (I don't know what "We only ever produce T." means in the comment), I'd argue that `T` could be bivariant here, but that's not an option nowadays (cc @nikomatsakis this may be an interesting edge case).

author: nikomatsakis

body:
@yoshuawuyts Ah, @matklad's comment is entirely correct, but note that it said `fn() -> T`, not `dyn Fn() -> T`. If I had to guess, maybe `fn` was typo'd as `Fn` and then the compiler asked for `dyn` to be added for the new, more explicit, trait object syntax.

Like @nikomatsakis said, `dyn Fn` needs to be replaced with `fn`.

<hr/>

`PhantomData<fn() -> T>` and `PhantomData<T>` have the same ("normal" aka "co-") variance, it's just that the former is more relaxed in terms of reasoning about drops (whereas the latter would be *needed* if you had, say,  an owning raw pointer to a heap-allocated `T` value, like `Box<T>` or even `Rc<T>`).

<hr/>

`PhantomData<dyn Fn() -> T>`, OTOH, being *a trait object*, is necessarily (because we know nothing of the concrete type, which may have arbitrary restrictions) invariant over `T` .
That makes it similar to `PhantomData<Cell<T>>` and `PhantomData<&'a mut T>`.

If `Pending<T>` was invariant over `T`, then  `Pending<&'static ()>` would not be able to become `Pending<&'a ()>` for some `'a` smaller than `'static`.

```suggestion
    pub unsafe fn get_uninit_unchecked(&mut self, index: usize) -> &mut MaybeUninit<T> {
```

There are two ways in which you can violate soundness with this method:

1. You provide `index` where `index >= self.capacity()`.
2. You do `let elem = vec.get_uninit_unchecked(index); *elem = MaybeUninit::uninit(); drop(vec[index]);`.

This is the part that will be removed after #71044 lands. Sorry. That should have been in the commit message along with `HACK`.

This is here because we want `join_state_into_successors` to have the same signature for both forward and backward analyses. A `ReadOnlyBodyAndCache` is required to access a basic block predecessors, but the current API requires that you *always* compute and cache the predecessor graph before creating a `ReadOnlyBodyAndCache`. This would be wasted work for the vast majority of dataflow analyses, which run forward.

FWIW, figuring this out how this was supposed to work caused me a great deal of consternation and was the motivation for #71044, which goes back to using `Body` everywhere.

In an initial version of #64566, I added an `assert` that fired when dataflow was run on a CFG with unreachable basic blocks. author: petrochenkov

body:
>They show up in the rustc code all over the place, but there is no real explanation to what they exactly control.

`is_like_msvc` and `is_like_windows` are some ad-hoc flags controlling target-dependent behavior (introduced in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/16156, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/25350).
Sometimes it may mean "uses Windows ABI", sometimes "the produced executable is PE/COFF", sometimes "search libraries in directories specific to visual studio", or something else like "uses PDB as debuginfo".

I'm not sure *all* of these aspects apply to UEFI, so enabling them may both fix something and break something.

These flags likely need to be split into multiple more specific flags, but nobody bothered to do it yet because we had only windows-msvc and windows-gnu targets until recently.

body:
I would prefer for us to detect these kind of cases proactively and give a more targeted error. In the case of

```rust
struct S0<T>(T);
impl<T> S0<T> {
    const C: S0<u8> = Self(0);

    fn foo() {
        Self(0);
    }
}
```

we should come up with a more extensive explanation of what `Self` resolves to, something closer to

```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> $DIR/issue-69306.rs:5:28
   |
LL | impl<T> S0<T> {
   |      - this type parameter
LL |     const C: S0<u8> = Self(0);
   |                       ---- ^ expected type parameter `T`, found integer
   |                       |
   |                       expected `T` because of this
   |
   = note: expected type parameter `T`
                        found type `{integer}`
note: `Self` resolves to `S0<T>`, which doesn't match `S0<{integer}>` becaue it is more general
   |
```

body:
This comment should be adjusted. I think it should be:

---

Returns an operand suitable for use as a call argument. This is almost always equivalent to `as_operand`, except for the particular case of passing values of (potentially) unsized types "by value" (see details below). 

As with `as_operand`, the operand returned from this function will *not be valid* after an `ExprKind::Scope` is passed, so do not return it from functions.

# Parameters of unsized types

We tweak the handling of parameters of unsized type slightly to avoid the need to create a local variable of unsized type. For example, consider this program:

```rust
fn foo(p: dyn Debug) { ... }

fn bar(box_p: Box<dyn Debug>) {
    foo(*p);
}
```

Ordinarily, for sized types, we would compile the call `foo(*p)` like so:

```rust
let tmp0 = *box_p; // tmp0 would be the operand returned by this function
call foo(tmp0)
```

But because the parameter to `foo` is of the unsized type `dyn Debug`, and because it is being moved the deref of a box, we compile it slightly differently. The temporary `tmp0` that we create *stores the entire box*, and the parameter to the call itself will be `*tmp0`:

```rust
let tmp0 = box_p;
call foo(*tmp0)
```

This way, the temporary `tmp0` that we create has type `Box<dyn Debug>`, which is sized. The value passed to the call (`*tmp0`) still has the `dyn Debug` type -- but the way that calls are compiled means that this parameter will be passed "by reference", meaning that we will actually provide a pointer to the interior of the box, and not move the `dyn Debug` value to the stack.

See #68034 for more details.

So the bug is about this line -- this gets the scope in which the returned value should be valid. The intent is to read the "enclosing scope at the time that `as_call_operand` was called. But because we are now recursing into scopes, what we're getting is an inner scope instead -- i.e., something specific to this particular operand.

Basically for a call, there are (at least) two scopes involved:

```
foo(    // <---------------+ scope for `foo(*x)`
  *x,   // scope for `*x`  |
) // <---------------------+
```

The `local_scope` as we initially call `as_call_operand` is the outer scope, the one for `foo(*x)`, but once we recurse, `local_scope` refers to `*x`. 

I'll push the commit I used to test this theory, which also fixes the problem. It basically just passes in `local_scope` as a parameter. Maybe it'd be better even to rename it to `call_scope` or something like that.

body:
I'm happy to dig in further, but I'd prefer to land this change in the meantime. 
The message starts with a disclaimer, it intentionally only suggests `use` instead of showing a potentially-incorrect path. So I think risk of confusion is low, and mentioning `use` is an important improvement.

This check currently happens very early in the parsing, so a naive mod existence checks at this stage would be unreliable and sensitive to order of definitions. A proper fix may be quite involved, e.g. create a "broken mod" AST node for a later pass to pick it up and scan modules after they're all parsed. That might take longer to implement, so the current PR is IMHO good to have in the meantime.

So what I'm thinking is something like this:

- We should have a new `ConstPropMode` which means that we can only propagate within the same `BasicBlock` that the local is assigned in.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4ca5fd2d7b6b1d75b6cb8f679e8523fb3e7b19e2/src/librustc_mir/transform/const_prop.rs#L768-L775

- Set that here for `LocalKind::Var`

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4ca5fd2d7b6b1d75b6cb8f679e8523fb3e7b19e2/src/librustc_mir/transform/const_prop.rs#L798

- I think we don't need this change then (but I'm not sure I completely understand why it's required currently in the PR).

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/71298/files#diff-9e103702275cbef342c2decd3395bf3bR818-R822

- Add a field to track what locals we need to forget at the end of a block here. (I recommend using `BitSet<Local>`)

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4ca5fd2d7b6b1d75b6cb8f679e8523fb3e7b19e2/src/librustc_mir/transform/const_prop.rs#L325-L338

- The logic around here needs to be adjusted to allow the mode but, in the new mode, call `BitSet<Local>::insert()` so that we know we need to remove the const value when the block completes.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4ca5fd2d7b6b1d75b6cb8f679e8523fb3e7b19e2/src/librustc_mir/transform/const_prop.rs#L859-L880

- As the last step in `visit_terminator()`, loop over every local we have to forget and call `self.remove_const(local)`.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4ca5fd2d7b6b1d75b6cb8f679e8523fb3e7b19e2/src/librustc_mir/transform/const_prop.rs#L901

I think most of the failing tests are because we aren't forgetting the values for variables when we should be which is having wacky effects on the MIR.

The thing is, from a dynamic perspective there is nothing wrong with a const that *points to* a mutable static. So I don't think we should check for it here.

The static checks do that as part of their approximation, sure, but quoting from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/49146#issuecomment-616301045
> Miri is perfectly capable of emitting an error when it encounters an illegal operation on a qualified value, and it can do so with no false positives. 

I agree with @ecstatic-morse that it *should* do so with no false positives. But failing with a const *refers to* (but does not read from) a mutable static is a false positive.

body:
> What about left?

Whoops, you're right. I've left left out.

> What about the other functions that your previous PR exposed to subst-carrying data which were previously guarded by that if you moved around?

The only reason I felt comfortable with doing this is `check_{unary, binary}_op` is only called from the `const_prop` method, so only `check_{unary, binary}_op` (and their callees) are newly exposed to subst-carrying data (speaking of which, I see `check_unary_op` also needs to be guarded because it evals its operand).

And what is even happening that we see uninitialized data, and that no assertion anywhere fires to detect that we run the engine on code it cannot run?

Per https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/71353#issuecomment-616550763, isn't it just the error message raised during validation that's suspicious? I'm not sure that there's really uninitialised data here. I'll chuck a debugger on and see where the Err is being raised.

body:
> And what is even happening that we see uninitialized data, and that no assertion anywhere fires to detect that we run the engine on code it cannot run? This is the most concerning part to me. Cc @oli-obk

I'm entirely confused by this issue. I don't like the fix in this PR, it doesn't address the issue, it just makes sure we don't run into it.

It should be perfectly possible to evaluate `std::ptr::null()` for unknown (but `Sized`!) `T`. I don't see why it's failing validation of all things. I'd understand it if we'd get a `TooGeneric` error due to layout computation bailing out or sth. I think this is a bug in validation.

After checking what causes "uninitialized raw ptr", I believe the fault is at https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/c6b55eed638db7db34e887ef255c765bc8910ec0/src/librustc_mir/interpret/place.rs#L307

well, not really, this is where I'd expect the `TooGeneric` error to come from, but `try_validation!` turns *every* error into a validation error: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/2dc5b602eee35d70e8e6e506a7ea07b6c7e0197d/src/librustc_mir/interpret/validity.rs#L54

We should probably not do that for any errors of the `InvalidProgramError` category: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/mir/interpret/enum.InterpError.html#variant.InvalidProgram (and we can probably ICE for a few other categories)
author: oli-obk

body:
Ah, good point -- probably `try_validation!` turns `TooGeneric` into a validation failure.

I propose `try_validation!` should take a pattern for the error it expects, and then probably just propagate other errors through unchanged. (A fancy version of the macro would allow giving multiple patterns with different validation messages, like [what we do here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/2dc5b602eee35d70e8e6e506a7ea07b6c7e0197d/src/librustc_mir/interpret/validity.rs#L362).)

Propagation is a bit risky because [of this catch here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/2dc5b602eee35d70e8e6e506a7ea07b6c7e0197d/src/librustc_mir/interpret/validity.rs#L673) which catches errors not caught elsewhere in a very coarse-grained way... but the error variants are specific enough that this is probably okay.

If @oli-obk 's theory is right that will turn the weird validation failure into an ICE (triggered [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/2dc5b602eee35d70e8e6e506a7ea07b6c7e0197d/src/librustc_mir/interpret/validity.rs#L841)), which is an improvement.

Using `as` to convert `i64` to `u64` wraps (i.e. takes the value mod 2^64) so doing a wrapping subtract after that operation computes the right value.

body: @RalfJung Could you say some more about how and why `Box` is special in Stacked Borrows? Could it be "just" another library type? Are `Vec` or `Rc` for example also special?
author: SimonSapin

body:
The *how*: `Box` is basically like `&mut` (except that unlike `&mut` we never add "protectors" for `Box`, but that's a detail).

The *why*: As far as I know, rustc emits `noalias` annotations for `Box`. This demonstrates that it is not "just another library type". Those annotations are incorrect unless our aliasing model (i.e., Stacked Borrows) actually treats `Box` special. Additionally, back when I started with Stacked Borrows, we also added `dereferencable` annotations. Right now [we do not do that any more](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/66645), but the plan is to start doing that again once LLVM weakened `dereferencable` semantics to mean "dereferencable on entry to the function" (as opposed to "dereferencable throughout the entire execution of the function", which is what it means now). That would be another way in which `Box` is not just a library type.

Long-term, the plan is to not make `Box` special but to make `Unique` special instead. At least, @Gankra told me that that was the plan. ;) But that is blocked on figuring out better how exactly we want it to be special.
author: RalfJung

body:
> Are Vec or Rc for example also special?

No, right now only `Box` is special.

Eventually, when `Unique` is special, that would be inherited by `Vec`. `Vec` is, in fact, the main motivation for making `Unique` special. See e.g. https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/71354.

body:
> Proc-macros shouldn't be any different to cdylibs and dylibs with regards to linking behavior

That was the problem 😉

TL;DR It's a hack.

Musl target is a "weirdo". Because of the legacy decisions it defaults to static linking so it cannot produce dylibs, cdylibs and proc-macros. Now lack of proc-macro support doesn't matter when cross-compiling from the host which supports them to musl.
It becomes difficult when using musl as the host toolchain. Since it defaults to static linking proc-macros don't work. To build them one had to use `target-feature=-crt-static` and lose ability to statically link binaries.
author: mati865

body:
@mati865 
First, musl toolchain actually supports statically linking self-contained `.so`s, despite the flag in `rustc` target spec saying otherwise, I tried it (at least with "hello world"-like examples).

Second, that doesn't mean that we *want* to use it for proc macros (as well as cdylibs and dylibs) at the same time as we are building a statically linked executable.

So, one common `RUSTFLAGS="-Ctarget-feature=+crt-static"` (or a target spec default) in this case brings collateral damage on the crates which it is not supposed to apply to.

I see multiple possible solutions here some of which could be more principled than what https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/69519 did.
- Automatically enable `-Ctarget-feature=-crt-static` for proc macro crates or all libraries in Cargo, modifying RUSTFLAGS. Question: how to opt-out?
- Introduce a new options `-Ctarget-feature=+crt-static-dylib` controlling static linking of libraries instead of `-Ctarget-feature=-crt-static`. It would almost never be used on Linux (not sure about windows-msvc and wasm).
- Keep the existing meaning of `crt-static`, but introduce a new option `-C disable-crt-static-for-dylibs` or something. Cargo would then use it for proc macro crates or all libraries. Question: how to opt-out?
- Ignore `+crt-static` for dylibs if the target doesn't support it. This is fragile, musl actually supports it despite the current value of the flag of the musl target spec. If the flag is enabled, proc macros will break.
- Ignore `+crt-static` for dylibs always. They are almost never used on Linux (not sure about windows-msvc and wasm). `+crt-static-dylib` looks strictly better.
author: petrochenkov

body: - Have two `crt-static` defaults in target specs - one for executables and one for libraries. Solves one half of the problem, but explicit `+crt-static` in RUSTFLAGS will still cause collateral damage.
author: petrochenkov

body: What user-level libraries will it statically link to other than the CRT? For `windows-msvc` `crt-static` *only* controls whether the CRT (consisting of the VC Runtime and the UCRT) is statically linked and nothing else is affected. body:
That argument is... a bit strange to me. I can call `mem::drop` myself without double-dropping, so if that was the problem, why wouldn't the compiler just apply the same rules for `Drop::drop`?

The answer is that *the type of `Drop::drop` is a lie*. That function is *not* like any other function that takes a mutable reference. Usually, a function taking `&mut T` borrows `T` and then it has to give back an intact `T` when the borrow is over. `Drop::drop`, on the other hand, partially *destroys* the `T`, and it may rely on the fact that no other method is called on this type any more after it returns. *That* is why it cannot be called directly.
author: RalfJung

body:
"destructor" could be another term we could use for "drop glue", but I am not sure if that isn't confusing as people might also think it refers to `Drop::drop`. But in that case we should later explain which of the two concepts that we explain in more detail, is meant by "destructor" -- or probably we should never use that term again, and only use it here in the introduction before we established the terminology.

In fact, that made me think of a structure like that:

> When a value is no longer needed, Rust will run a "destructor" on that value.
>
>  [...]
>
> Destructors in Rust consist of two components:
> * implementations of the `Drop` trait, that customize the destructor for values of a particular type.
> * the compiler-generated "drop glue", that automatically calls `Drop::drop` on a value and then recursively does the same for all its fields.

So to avoid the cyclic dependency, we basically introduce both terms at the same time. What do you think?

body:
> Hm, I was trying to capture what made ManuallyDrop special so it would be easier to compare to MaybeUninit,

In terms of [my experimental terminology](https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2018/08/22/two-kinds-of-invariants.html) -- `MaybeUninit` has a trivial validity and safety invariant (as in, the invariant is satisfied by any sequence of bytes, including uninitialized bytes); `ManuallyDrop` inherits both of them from `T`.

But I am not sure what the best way is to explain that...
author: RalfJung

body:
Hm, IMO "initialisation invariant" is quite confusing in this context, for two reasons:

1) We use "uninitialised" to mean a specific state of memory, which is a different state from "not meeting the initialisation invariant". For example, for `MaybeUninit`, "uninitialised" *does* meet the initialisation invariant.

2) "Initialised" normally means the state between the value being constructed and its destruction. However, for `ManuallyDrop` we have the constraint that the contained value must continue to meet the initialisation invariant... after it is dropped.

If "initialisation invariant" is the terminology we have settled on for now, then I think we need to call out the above ambiguities.
author: Diggsey

body:
I agree that "initialization invariant" is not a good term for the reasons you gave.

> However, for ManuallyDrop we have the constraint that the contained value must continue to meet the initialisation invariant... after it is dropped.

Not really -- after `mem::drop::<ManuallyDrop<T>>(x)`, `x` is gone and its initialization does not matter any more.

The inherent method in `ManuallyDrop` does not drop the `ManuallyDrop`, as far as the language definition is concerned.

The reasoning is that until very recently, we always spilled function call arguments to temporaries (basically, `add(1u8, 2u8)` would become `_tmp0 = 1u8; _tmp1 = 2u8; add(_tmp0, _tmp1`). The reasons for doing that aren't terribly important. 

The only caveat here is an unstable feature called `unsized_locals`. You can read more about what changed in #71170 but the TLDR is that in a very niche situation, we don't follow this exact pattern. I think this is unimportant for const-prop because 1) this is a very specific situation and 99.999% of Rust code in the wild is not going to do this and 2) I suspect const-prop can't handle derefs to unsized locals anyway so it would have given up before even reaching this line of code.
author: wesleywiser

body:
Here's a brain dump about the scalar thing:

Currently, we only have a way to create consts from scalars. The representation of values in miri that we care about fall into a few cases:

- [`Operand`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_mir/interpret/enum.Operand.html)
  - This enum is the most general representation of values in miri. It abstracts over both direct values and values help indirectly in memory.
  - This is the `Op` in `OpTy`.

  - `Immediate`
    - This represents a value directly. It can be 0, 1, or 2 individual `Scalar`s. You're probably thinking "why two?", that's because checked math is very common and is represented as a tuple of `(over/under-flowed: bool, result: integer)` and having the values not spill into Indirect memory significantly improves performance. 

  - `Indirect`
    - This represents all other values and is backed by an allocation somewhere in miri. This could either be because a user requested it (eg `let x = Box::new(4u8);`) or because the value doesn't fit in an `Immediate`. 

This code checks for the very common case of an argument that is expressed by one scalar but misses the case where it fits in two scalars. Unifying the treatment of `Operands` as @oli-obk mentioned in your original PR would be a good way to handle that without duplicating code.

So? We need to allocate anyway so it doesn't matter if it happens in the `or_insert` call or `push`. Using `Option` means the empty case is serialized as `a: null` rather than `a: []`. I don't see the advantage to that. > What would be the gain of using a `BTreeMap` btw? Do we really care about being more deterministic?

We need determinism for reproducible builds. Admittedly it looks like `FxHashMap` is deterministic enough for that but I really don't like relying on that. Having it alphabetized also makes it easier to debug and compare changes made to the alias list.

body:
So, `eliminate_input` is a helper method to delete a column from the "compatibility matrix" which tracks which arguments could be passed to which parameters.  However, as we eliminate those columns, we still need to know which columns correspond to which original parameters.

For example, suppose I have `fn myFunc(a: A, b: B, c: C)`, and you call it as `fn myFunc(B {}, A {}, C {})`.

The compatibility matrix would be (only T's are shown for clarity)
```
[., T, .]
[T, ., .]
[., ., T]
```

and the `input_indexes` collection (ii) would be `[1,2,3]`.

After we detect that a and b are swapped, we eliminate that row and column, and end up with
```
[T]
```

but to know that that single column corresponds to the third input, `input_indexes` is `[3]`.

I can't remember why, but at some point we were eliminating columns past the end of `input_indexes`, and I threw this in to unblock me while I finished the rest of the algorithm.  I'll investigate whether it's still needed.

body:
I think I would prefer not to add the new method. The other `try` iterator methods (try_fold and try_for_each) expose a tangible new capability over the non-try (fold, for_each) because the non-try do not have an ability to early terminate. But Iterator::find_map is already entirely about early termination. In find_map the closure is supposed to return Some if you want to early terminate and None to keep iterating, and find_map's return value gives the thing you early terminated with if any, whether that's an error or an object if you want. The proposed try_find_map is the same but with a "transposed" interpretation of the closure:

```rust
iter.try_find_map(|s| parse_even(s))

// equivalent to:
iter.find_map(|s| parse_even(s).transpose()).transpose()
```

All in all I don't think the benefit is there more than e.g. try_map, try_filter, try_filter_map, try_skip_while, try_scan, try_any, try_partition etc, and I'm not on board with more in this direction just for small convenience. I think the fallible-iterator crate is a suitable place for this kind of thing.

I would be happy to take the try_find fixes though: the doc fix, removed type parameter, and reduced parametricity.

body:
Looks like it the deaggregator "unpeels" empty types now, so this ZST doesn't need to be stored anymore (not that it matters too much for ZSTs).

Note that the generator transform uses the liveness dataflow analysis, which doesn't work correctly after the deaggregator has run - it treats every assignment to a field of an aggregate as a use of the base local, which may lead to locals being considered live up to the function's entry point. This does not cause unsoundness here, but it might cause some size regressions. However it looks like the `MaybeRequiresStorage` analysis fully mitigates this effect by only requiring storage for a local after the first field of the aggregate is written.

body:
There is indeed a bug here. I'm missing a `seek_before_primary_effect(terminator_loc)`.

The comment below addresses your broader concern. If there's **N** locations in a block, we also have **N** dataflow effects in the block (as long as we don't use "before" effects). That means **N+1** possibly unique dataflow states, since you need to consider boundary conditions (before the first effect is applied, after the last effect is applied). If we seek before all possible locations, then seek after the final location (via `seek_to_block_end`), we will have observed all of them.

body:
The previous analysis cared about them because it's possible for something to require storage even if it's been de-initialized. The address could have been captured from a borrow and unsafe code could use that to re-initialize the value.

By the definition of this MaybeInitializedLocals analysis, we shouldn't care about it, but we should still assume in the generator transform that anything borrowed and MaybeStorageLive might still require storage, even if it's not initialized.

My assertion, which perhaps should have been stated explicitly as it relies on some yet-to-be-documented MIR invariants, is that `live_across_yield` as currently formulated is always a strict subset of `storage_live`: 

A local cannot be borrowed before it is `storage_live` and `borrowed` already invalidates borrows when it sees `StorageDead`. Likewise, a local cannot be initialized before it is marked `StorageLive` and it cannot be used (marking it live) after it is `StorageDead`.

Therefore, there is no point intersecting with `storage_live`. Perhaps it would be good to `debug_assert` this to be sure? This is somewhat related to #68622.

body:
> Wasn't libcore/liballoc already using that?

Using what?

libstd/liballoc/libcore (and all of rustc really except for the test suite) should only be using the sound version of the feature. After all, we don't want unsound code in our standard library or the compiler.  So clearly `unsized_locals` should not be enabled. Does this make sense so far?

The claim, back when passing unsized parameters to functions was carved out as a "soundly implementable subset", was that this would suffice for what libstd is doing. So assuming that claim is correct, no further changes should be needed to disable `unsized_locals`.

However, the bootstrap compiler does not understand `unsized_fn_params`, so we still have to enable the unsound `unsized_locals` *but only when building the standard library with the bootstrap compiler*.

TL;DR we now manually add dllexport/dllimport.

With version-scripts LD sort of scans the symbols to decide when to automatically add dllexport.
With `.def` it doesn't use automatic dllexport but dllexport can be manually enabled by what this PR does or writing `DATA` next to the symbol on the list.

Previously most of the tests worked before because of automatic dllimport, broken tests were using statics which don't work with automatic dllimport.

body:
I believe these braces you have added here have no effect.

The current r-value lifetime rules will cause the lock() temporary to be dropped at the end of the evaluation of the expression; we do not extend it to the end of the containing block (which in this case would be the `fn` body of `decode_expn_id` itself).

(The place where you *do* need such braces is when you `let`-bind the value, as you do below with `let mut expns = outer_expns.lock();`.)

----

I would say that if your goal is to make the dynamic extent of the `lock()` temporary as clear as possible to future readers of this code, then I would keep the braces but I would also add a let-binding of the temporary, so that the braces are meaningful.

(The demo also points out a potentially surprising difference in the semantics of `if` vs `if let` in terms of what the r-value lifetime rules yield, but that is just a side-note; it does not contradict my main point that these braces have no effect.)

body:
So right now, this will return `false` for types such as `[i64; 4]` and `&str`. This is correct at the moment because `is_structural_eq_shallow` is always used in conjunction with type visitors that handle those cases separately, only invoking the query for `TyKind::Adt`. We could just document this fact and call it a day, or switch this query to accept only `TyKind::Adt`s, but I think it will be less prone to misuse if we handle the fundamental types inside the query instead of making the caller do it. 

If you agree, there's two ways to accomplish this, we could either move this special-casing into the query itself or implement `StructuralEq` for fundamental types. Your point about function pointers suggests that we just do the first one, since we can't cover all the fundamental types via trait impls anyway.

body:
My main reaction is: I think you're rightfully worried about the method being prone to misuse.

 * In particular, I'm worried that the doc-comment you've put above `is_structurally_eq_shallow` might actually detract from readers' understanding of the code as written. (It adopts a relatively simple specification ("when this returns true, you can conclude X; when it returns false, you cannot conclude anything"), which is what led me to say "can't we just land this code as is, and expand it later?"). But as you point out, all the current call-sites are making **stronger** assumptions about its behavior ("when given an ADT, then true implies X, and false implies not-X").

My first thought is: It would be nice to decide what interface we want, and then have the calls match it. But then my second thought is: It seems silly to put the effort into making all the call-sites handle the general case when they *know* that the method will produce usable results immediately when given an ADT.

In the long-term, you're probably right that we should move the special-casing into the query itself, so that it will handle any input `ty` properly.

However, I do not want to block this PR on that addition. For various reasons (such as ease of identifying source of performance regressions), I think we should land this PR as is, with an addition to the doc-comment saying that the `is_structurally_eq_*` methods happen to be precise when given an ADT. (i.e., I am advising that we indeed "just document this fact and call it a day", except I'm only saying "call it a day" for the short term; maybe add a FIXME for the longer term goal.)

We should probably ignore the error here, as AFAICT it's not guaranteed that this will succeed. In particular, my manpage for ftruncate64 says:

> For non-XSI-compliant systems, the POSIX standard allows two behaviors for ftruncate() when length exceeds the file  length  (note that  truncate() is not specified at all in such an environment): either returning an error, or extending the file.  Like most UNIX implementations, Linux follows  the  XSI  requirement  when dealing  with native filesystems.  However, some nonnative filesystems do not permit truncate() and ftruncate() to be used to extend a file beyond its current length:  a  notable  example  on Linux is VFAT.  


It's also true that I think we're changing the behavior slightly -- if the write_all call fails for whatever reason (e.g. network disconnect on a network file system) this will now create a zero-filled file rather than one with not yet all the bytes written. I'm not sure that this is the right thing to do.

body: In the literature I've read, "copy propagation" is a general idea, not a specific algorithm. If you have a counter-example, I would be happy to see it, although I feel quite strongly that my interpretation in correct. This PR, much like the existing `copy_prop` pass in `rustc`, is a very limited form of copy propagation. The "place unification" algorithm in #47954 and #71003 is a more robust approach, and I will change this comment to link to it. Unlike copy propagation, "place unification", which I've been calling it "variable coalescing" because of the similar step during [register allocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_allocation#Coalescing), is not a term of art.

body:
I see what you mean, but referencing `--extern` is a bit obscure. `--extern` is not typically seen or used by end users, and they may not even be aware of the option. Talking about "dependencies" is a bit higher level and more directly what the programmer is going to be using.

I'm not sure what you mean by `extern crate`. From my point of view, I see this lint as being responsible for highlighting a mismatch between the build system dependencies (as manifest by `--extern`) and what the source says - ie, does the source reference an external dependency? By this standard `extern crate` doesn't count because it's necessarily part of the sources - and we have `UNUSED_EXTERN_CRATES` for flagging those. Also I don't think it can actually add a new dependency can it? It's just a reference to one in the same manner as `use`, and so needs a corresponding `--extern`? (I guess std, core, etc excepted, but I think its reasonable for them to be exempt from this lint too.)

While `--extern` can refer to non-existent crates, and I think its useful to report that, it should never happen in practice unless the build system is broken, or you're manually invoking `rustc`.

EDIT: I re-read the [reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/extern-crates.html). I guess another option is to warn about unused things in the external prelude which would include both `--extern` and `extern crate`, and so the same diagnostic would cover both cases. But that would also warn about `core` and `std` if they're implicitly added (which I don't think we'd want to warn about), and overall seems more complex as it would have to deal with `as foo` aliases as well. I'm not sure if this is what you were getting at, but I thought it was worth noting.

body: I don't care so much about `cloned` vs `clone`, but there do seem to be some calls to `clone` for `Copy` types, which [clippy will lint against](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/pull/602). body:
So, something is wrong here. I have a generator where `discr_ty` here returns a 32bit type, but then the MIR `Discriminant` statement is used to put this into a 64bit type. IOW, the MIR is ill-formed, as far as I can tell.

[Here's the code](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=75c57a7439eb29b9f9ba346ab5d565ca), and here the relevant MIR snippet:
```
fn basic::{{closure}}#0(_1: std::pin::Pin<&mut [generator@src/main.rs:37:15: 37:25 {usize, ()}]>, _2: ()) -> std::ops::GeneratorState<usize, ()> {
    let mut _0: std::ops::GeneratorState<usize, ()>; // return place in scope 0 at src/main.rs:37:15: 37:25
    let mut _3: ();                      // in scope 0 at src/main.rs:37:18: 37:18
    let mut _4: isize;                   // in scope 0 at src/main.rs:37:15: 37:25

    bb0: {
        _4 = discriminant((*(_1.0: &mut [generator@src/main.rs:37:15: 37:25 {usize, ()}]))); // scope 0 at src/main.rs:37:15: 37:25
        switchInt(move _4) -> [0u32: bb1, 1u32: bb3, 3u32: bb2, otherwise: bb4]; // scope 0 at src/main.rs:37:15: 37:25
    }
```
Notice `_4` is ptr-sized, but (if I interpret everything correctly), `discr_ty` for that generator is `u32` -- that's what my logs say, anyway:
```
[TRACE rustc_mir::interpret::operand] tag value: 0x00
[TRACE rustc_mir::interpret::operand] discriminant type: u32
thread 'rustc' panicked at 'assertion failed: `(left == right)`
  left: `Size { raw: 4 }`,
 right: `Size { raw: 8 }`: Size mismatch when writing bits', /home/r/src/rust/rustc.2/src/libstd/macros.rs:16:9
```

author: RalfJung

body:
Well I've updated the comment in the code as discussed.

> SeqCst is hardly ever required.

You missed off the second part of that sentence 😛 I said SeqCst *or that the code needs to change*. I think the only part I'm disagreeing with you on is that it is generally sufficient to use `AcqRel` everywhere and be confident it's correct: in my experience as soon as more than one atomic variable is involved, you can't get away with that simplification anymore.

With a single atomic variable and AcqRel everywhere, the complexity grows linearly with the amount of code, and things are still fairly intuitive. Once you have more than one atomic variable using AcqRel, the complexity grows exponentially: each atomic variable will have some order on operations, but this may be inconsistent with the order observed by accesses to a different atomic variable.

Each Acquire/Release pair only adds a single ordering constraint between two threads. With multiple threads and multiple atomics, this inevitably leaves the set of possible executions wildly unconstrained. SeqCst is unique in that it enforces a total ordering across *all* atomic accesses, not just the variable being accessed, and so it is capable of placing constraints between multiple threads at once. As a result it can be much easier to reason about, even if a weaker set of memory orderings may be possible, simply because there are exponentially fewer possible executions.
author: Diggsey

body:
> Each Acquire/Release pair only adds a single ordering constraint between two threads. With multiple threads and multiple atomics, this inevitably leaves the set of possible executions wildly unconstrained. SeqCst is unique in that it enforces a total ordering across all atomic accesses, not just the variable being accessed, and so it is capable of placing constraints between multiple threads at once. As a result it can be much easier to reason about, even if a weaker set of memory orderings may be possible, simply because there are exponentially fewer possible executions.

Reasoning based on `SeqCst` requires reasoning by case distinction: did this go first or that? That is the unique guarantee that `SeqCst` provides. This is inherently exponential in nature, as there are exponentially many ways that a bunch of accesses could be ordered.

There is a better way to reason about concurrent code, which is by thinking of everything in terms of ownership transfer. (And in my research I have shown that [ownership transfer is really all you need](https://people.mpi-sws.org/~dreyer/papers/iris-ground-up/paper.pdf).) That avoids the exponential blowup. And for ownership transfer, `AcqRel` is sufficient. Thus, I disagree with your statement that the guarantee `SeqCst` adds actually helps simplify reasoning in general. (Well, you said "*can* be much easier", but it is hard to argue against there being cases where indeed it is simpler. If your statement is that such cases *exist*, I cannot disagree. I am arguing they are not common.) Only rarely does reasoning actually require doing a case distinction which of two operations went first, and only then `SeqCst` should be used.

Anyway, we are digressing. I'd love to have this discussion with you via a better medium than text at some point. :)

body:
(First of all let's cc @RalfJung for their UB expertise)

Hmmm, I think we can make _fewer_ changes: **I don't think that the definition for `Arc` needs to be changed**; AFAIK, the "only" / main offender here is a `Weak` calling `.inner()` while a unique `Arc` is around, since that `Arc` believes it is allowed to do whatever it wants with the data, when, because of that callable `.inner()` (transitively yielding a `&'_ T` _shared_ reference to the `data`) on a simultaneous `Weak` instance, it cannot.

So I suggest _keeping everything as it was_, except for the signature of the returned value of `.inner()`, which should be changed to return an `Option<_>` of:

  - either `&'_ ArcInner<UnsafeCell<MaybeUninit<T>>` (the `MaybeUninit` part setting things up for further evolutions, such as the one in your other PR),

  - or, more simply, `&'_ ArcInner<1-ZST>` (which would make `.inner()` effectively equivalent to a `.counters()` 
getter returning a `struct Counters<'inner> { strong: &'inner AtomicUsize, weak: &'inner AtomicUsize }`, which is fine since that's exactly what `.inner()` should be doing before knowing that `strong ≥ 1`!).

In both cases the core idea is that a `Weak` gets to look at its counters, mainly the `strong` one, before ever trying to assert anything about the `.data` / to peek at it. This way, a unique `Arc` owner can effectively take ownership of the `ArcInner`'s `.data` by clearing that `.strong` counter, so as to no longer worry about remaining `Weak`s.

___

Finally, remains the question of what the fields of `Weak` ought to be. Given that the pointer may already be dangling, and that therefore the blessed way to dereference that pointer is through the guarded `.inner()` getter, I'd say that we could let the field(s) remain as is. If, on the other hand, we really want to enforce / express at the type-level that using that getter is mandatory, we could change `Weak` to become:

```diff
+ struct ErasedPayload;
+ type Counters = ArcInner<ErasedPayload>; // thanks to `#[repr(C)]`-ness of `ArcInner`

struct Weak<T : ?Sized> {
-   ptr: NonNull<ArcInner<T>>,
+   ptr: NonNull<Counters>,
+   _phantom: PhantomData<ArcInner<T>>,
}
```

> if `GLOBAL_PANIC_COUNT` is zero, `LOCAL_PANIC_COUNT` will be zero.

This is a very strong statement to make, in particular about relaxed atomics! It took me some time to actually follow the argument here. You cannot, in general, relate the content of two *different* locations when you use relaxed accesses. In particular, "`GLOBAL_PANIC_COUNT` is zero" is an odd statement as atomics can appear to have different values in different threads. The only reason it works here is that one of the two is thread-local.  I was also confused at first because `decrease` decrements `GLOBAL` first, so there is a time when `GLOBAL` is already zero for the current thread but `LOCAL` is still 1.

So what about

> In any particular thread, if *that thread* currently views `GLOBAL_PANIC_COUNT` as being zero, then `LOCAL_PANIC_COUNT` *in that thread* is zero. This invariant holds *before* and *after* `increase` and `decrease`, but not necessarily during their execution.

Also, it would be good to explain in a comment why accessing an atomic global (potentially subject to contention)  is faster than accessing a non-atomic thread local. That is rather non-intuitive IMO -- I would have expected the exact opposite.

Good point.

This function encodes a code point in [generalized UTF-8](https://simonsapin.github.io/wtf-8/#generalized-utf8). For surrogate code points, the resulting byte sequence is not well-formed UTF-8 and therefore not valid `str`. The return type should be changed to `&mut [u8]` and the `from_utf8_unchecked` call moved to `char::encode_utf8`.

body:
So, currently we take the bounds from associated types and we "flatten" them onto the trait, and then we have this filtering logic that pulls them back out.

I've been wanting to experiment with a change where we do **not** do that. i.e., `tcx.predicates_of(trait_def_id)` would *not* include the bounds declared on associated types. Instead, you would explicitly invoke `tcx.pedicates_of(assoc_item_def_id)`.

We would modify the WF checks for an impl to explicitly prove the `tcx.predicates_of(assoc_item_def_id)` to be true. 

When we go to prove whether `T::Foo: Bar`, we would just check the `predicates_of` for `T::Foo`.

Obviously if we just did this, it would be backwards incompatible, since people might have explicitly written `where Self::Foo: Bar` on the trait today (as you point out in your comment). We could fix this by modifying that last point so that we take into account *either* things written on the trait (as this code here does) as well as the `predicates_of(assoc_item_def_id)`.

The motivation here would be two-fold:

* It would eliminate some of the O(n^2) behavior that @eddyb observed in the WF code. Right now, every time we prove that `T: Foo` is well-formed, we *also* prove that projections meet their bounds, but that seems excessive. We should be able to prove that exactly once at the impl level.
* It seems more compatible with GATs to me -- the where-clauses on an associated item may have additional generics in scope, and this version I am proposing here aligns naturally with that. Otherwise, we have to expand things to more complex `for<...>` predicates and that seems silly to me.

Thoughts? I can write-up an MCP and try to mentor someone to experiment with it (or maybe you want to look into it).
author: nikomatsakis

body:
"Might not"? As in, you're not sure? I have to admit I'm not, I'd have to go review what kind of syntax we permit. But I think that indeed the problems do not arise, as one cannot write "general where clauses" that refer to the `impl Trait`, right? Well, maybe you can write something like `type Foo<T: Eq> where Self: Bar = impl Baz`?

In that case, I'd prefer to convert the filter-map to an assertion.

body:
So there are a couple problems with doing it here; one is specific to `write_vectored`, and the other applies to all uses of this technique:

- Because our input is (equivalent to) `&[&[u8]]`, the only way to prepend our pre-buffered data would be allocating a new `Vec<&[u8]>`, which we want to avoid for hopefully obvious reasons. This problem doesn't apply to `write` or `write_all`, because our input is `&[u8]`, which means we can construct a `[&[u8]; 2]` to send to `write_vectored`.
- The key difference between `flush_buf` and `write` is that `write` makes at-most 1 attempt, whereas `flush_buf` has to loop until the buffer is empty or an error occurs. This isn't insurmountable, but it means that `flush_buf` has to be "vector aware", so that it can make looping calls to `write_vectored` but STOP when the writes transition to new data.

That being said, I'm definitely in favor of trying to update `BufWriter` and `LineWriter` to use this vector optimization, but I think it's out of scope for this PR.
author: Lucretiel

body: Another argument in favor of this is my proposal to replace `Vec<u8>` with `VecDeque<u8>` in `BufWriter`. This is a circular buffering that would eliminate the need for internal data copies in `BufWriter`, and substantially simplify the implementation of `flush_buf`. One of the downsides is that it means that the buffer can be "split", when the circular buffer wraps around the edge; vectored writes would mitigate this issue.

body:
- Regarding using the buffer as scratch space. Suppose we've buffered `"AAAA"`, and suppose that a write comes in for `"BBBB
CCC"`. If we append `"BBBB
"` to the buffer, we *must* report that we've consumed 5 bytes to the caller, by (at some point) returning `Ok(5)`. This means that, if the call to `inner.write("AAAABBBB
")` returns an error, we either have to silently drop that error, or remove the `"BBBB
"` from the buffer. Additionally, we have to make sure that we retry `Ok(2)` (because we only wrote pre-buffered data) but *don't* retry `Ok(6)` (because we should aim to make at-most 1 attempt to write new data).
- Regarding vectored writes: I agree, it's difficult to reconcile vectored writes with the behavior of LineBuffer. A reasonable behavior would be to disable them entirely, and allow it to simply forward to write. However, I'm assuming that users who want to combine vectored writes with `LineWriter` "know what they're doing", and so the behavior I've implemented tries to find the best balance of directly forwarding writes, without a lot of complex processing in the middle, with doing what you'd expect a `LineWriter` to do. It's worth noting that in the (presumably) common case that the buffers with newlines are terminated by them, the logic as-implemented exactly matches `write`.
- `LineWriter` doesn't have anything to do with unix pipelines; it's completely destination agnostic. It can be used to write to pipes, or to files, or to TCP sockets, or anything else. The only thing it's supposed to do is be a variant `BufWriter` that sends data to the wrapper writer when a newline comes through. The rest of the behavior about trying not to write partial lines, and trying only to write at newline boundaries, are design decisions I've made that I think represent best practice for a writer of this type.
- Related to what you're talking about is *specifically* what stdout should be doing. This pull request is preliminary work required for a future Pull Request for #60673, which aims to enable line-buffered vs block-buffered mode for stdout, which will (presumably) be set by default based on the tty status of stdout (and something similar on windows).

body:
> This means that, if the call to inner.write("AAAABBBB\n") returns an error, we either have to silently drop that error, or remove the "BBBB\n" from the buffer. 

I was thinking of the latter, which should be a fairly cheap operation, only the length needs to be changed on the buffer.

> Related to what you're talking about is specifically what stdout should be doing.

Not necessarily. If you have a linewriter wrapping a pipe fd then you only get atomic write guarantees up to `PIPE_BUF`. So if the expected behavior of LineWriter is to "write one line at a time" then aggregating multiple lines into a single write could violate the expectation of getting your lines written atomically. If too many lines get aggregated this can lead to unintentional interleaving (which looks a lot like tearing) in the pipe.
So in some circumstances it may make sense to deaggregate lines into multiple smaller writes (by doing short writes, no need to do multiple write calls internally) to provide per-line atomicity. Especially when we already have (partial) lines buffered from a previous write.

This isn't specific to stdout, it's useful for any kind of concurrent writing of line-based output. If you use a logger which has thread-local `LineWriter<&File/Pipe/whatever>` instances then avoiding line interleaving requires atomicity. Note that there is no locking.

> LineWriter doesn't have anything to do with unix pipelines; it's completely destination agnostic. It can be used to write to pipes, or to files, or to TCP sockets, or anything else. 

Indeed, it's not possible to get any atomicity guarantees from sockets under concurrent access. But regular files in append mode and pipes do offer some atomicity and it would be nice if linewriter could preserve those properties.

body:
My thinking would be that that use case should be handled by another `Write` adapter, or even a dedicated type. Certainly `LineBuffer` shouldn't change its behavior in the presence of environment variable or things like that. The `write` contract doesn't claim to provide "atomicity", because it doesn't prescribe what device is being wrapped. It just describes a composable method by which many write calls may be made, and a consistent state be retained even in the presence of partial writes or failures. If your use cases involves shared access to a single writable handle (atypical, because `Write` takes methods by `&mut self`), that would call for an adapter that caps write lengths (perhaps returning an error for too-large writes).

It's worth remembering that, if any data has been buffered, atomicity has already been lost, because the only ways for partial lines to be buffered are:

- The user made more than one write call.
- The device wrote less than a full line.

In the former case, the user plainly doesn't want atomic line writes, and in the latter case, a separate wrapper should be used to reject writes entirely that are too long.
author: Lucretiel

body:
> My thinking would be that that use case should be handled by another Write adapter,

But if you want line-based atomicity you need to search your input buffers for the right place to split the writes, so it would mostly be replicating the string scanning that LineWriter already does anyway.

> atypical, because Write takes methods by &mut self)

`impl<'_> Write for &'_ File`, thus having concurrent writers for any file descriptor is part of the standard library.

> In the former case, the user plainly doesn't want atomic line writes

Not necessarily. They could be expecting linewriter to provide that atomicity. If you do

```rust
writer.write(b"foo")?;
writer.write(b"bar")?;
writer.write(b"\n")?;
```

Then it will do it in a single syscall as you'd expect it. It's atomic on a good day.


> The device wrote less than a full line.

Not all types of file descriptors encounter short writes. At least linux akes an effort¹ to make regular file writes an all-or-nothing affair and for pipes there's the above-mentioned `PIPE_BUF` guarantee. Perhaps the pipe case can be covered by making an attempt to search for a newline within `capacity` bytes. I.e. if the BufWriter capacity is set to 8KiB and a caller passes a 32KiB of data then LineWriter it will do a short write for the first N lines that fit into 8KiB and only do a longer unbuffered write if it can't find one in that window.

Then the stdout implementation could probe if the file descriptor is a pipe and set the buffer size accordingly to `PIPE_BUF`, which will then be taken as a hint to deaggregate lines if needed.
An explicit parameter would work too (0 = no short writes for deaggregation).
Of course this is just a nice-to-have. But in my experience interleaved lines from multithreaded logging is a nuisance that can be avoided exactly this way.


¹ I say effort because there have been bugs and some network filesystems where that isn't the case. But local filesystems uphold this.

body:
When using `println!`, one desirable property is that the formatted output is
written using a single syscall. To take advantage of write atomicity, and avoid
interleaving the output with that from other processes that might be sharing
the same stdout.

The implementation here performs two syscalls whenever there are any formatting
operations in `println!`. The presence of terminal `\n` triggers the flush of
existing buffer content and then the final string with a newline is flushed
separately.

For example, `println!("Hello {}!", "world");`, leads to:

```
write(1, "Hello world", 11)             = 11
write(1, "!\n", 2)                      = 2
```

body:
Hmm. It's a good point. The problem is this:

Suppose that, as a solution (in your example), we buffer the second print, so that we can do the whole thing in a single write. At that point, we are *obligated* to return an Ok(2), because we have "successfully" written 2 bytes (by adding them to the buffer). This means that we can't actually attempt to send the byte to the underlying device, because if the device returns an error, we'd have to ignore that error (or save it and return it on the *next* write), which (along with extra, unnecessary data buffering) is something I was trying to avoid.

One workaround to this would be to buffer the data, attempt a write, and if the write returns an error, remove that data from the buffer. However, in that case, if the first write returns Ok(12) (representing "Hello World!") and the second write returns an error, there's no way to report a consistent result to the caller without also suppressing that error.

That being said, this problem probably *can* be addressed in the `write_all` specialization (used by default `write_fmt`), since it's not necessary to try to preserve a recoverable / knowable state in the event of an error there, like it is with `write`. I'll see about retooling `write_all` a bit to address this concern.

body:
I am trying to decide whether it is not intuitive for `fn next_id` to take a `span` as a parameter.

I think I understand the *intent* you have here: Every call to `next_id` is matched up with some portion of the HIR that is being generated via the lowering of the AST, and each such portion of the HIR is meant to always have a span associated with it. So in that sense, it makes sense to pass along the `span` so that you can enforce the invariant that all HIR entries have a span.

But at the same time, when I *read* the invocations written as `self.next_id(span)`, my own intuitive reading is "this is generating an `id` *from* the span somehow" (which is certainly not what is happening).

I'll keep musing on this. In the meantime, I would suggest you add a doc-comment to `fn next_id` saying what the `span` parameter is. (I also played with the idea of suggesting renaming the method, but I wasn't really happy with any of the alternatives I came up with...)

body:
Okay, so this sheds some more light as to why we use two-sided index. If we take a look at the save-analysis generated with this patch, we can see:
```
    {
      "attributes": [],
      "children": [],
      "decl_id": null,
      "docs": "",
      "id": {
        "index": 5,
        "krate": 0
      },
      "kind": "Local",
      "name": "world",
      "parent": null,
      "qualname": "world$18",
      "sig": null,
      "span": {
        "byte_end": 147,
        "byte_start": 142,
        "column_end": 14,
        "column_start": 9,
        "file_name": "src/tools/rls/tests/fixtures/common/src/main.rs",
        "line_end": 12,
        "line_start": 12
      },
      "value": "&str"
    },
    {
      "attributes": [],
      "children": [],
      "decl_id": null,
      "docs": "",
      "id": {
        "index": 5,
        "krate": 0
      },
      "kind": "Local",
      "name": "bar2",
      "parent": null,
      "qualname": "bar2$21",
      "sig": null,
      "span": {
        "byte_end": 207,
        "byte_start": 203,
        "column_end": 13,
        "column_start": 9,
        "file_name": "src/tools/rls/tests/fixtures/common/src/main.rs",
        "line_end": 15,
        "line_start": 15
      },
      "value": "Bar"
```

That's two "definitions", which have the same `def_id`. This is the reason why `client_highlight` fails as above. Informally, these are definitions in the name resolution sense (which don't have a separate DefId IIUC) and not item-like sense (which should have DefId). For the former, save-analysis used a negated index, so it created a *fake* def ids for those.

Because of this, I think we should retain the old behaviour for now (synthesizing `rls_data::Id` using negative indexing of `HirId`/`NodeId` as a numeric value) in case we don't have a `LocalDefId` for a given `HirId`.

```suggestion
or constants. This limitation exists to prevent the creation of constants that

type, you could modify the value through that reference, making the constant
essentially mutable. While there could be a more fine-grained scheme in the future
that allows mutable references if they aren't "leaked" to the final value, a more
```
