body:
I think we should take a different approach - I'd rather we avoid hard-coding `std` type names in the compiler (the compiler shouldn't need to be updated when `std` is changed for this diagnostic to continue to work) and I think we can make this more general, so it works for more than just `std`.

---

As you note in the PR description, we do Levenshtein matching on things that are already in-scope and suggest fixes in that case. We also already have suggestions for things that aren't in scope but where the name matches exactly.

The snippet below is where the compiler decides to make "did you mean to import this" suggestions:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/50c0192c64241d723066add22c53d472e2b9cba9/src/librustc_resolve/diagnostics.rs#L660-L693

On line 660 is where it checks for an exact match - I'd experiment with doing a exact match *or* checking for a Levenshtein distance from that name that's under some threshold (look into `lev_distance` and `find_best_match_for_name` to see what can be re-used). I'd hope that would detect cases like this where we can import a name that's very similar. Alternatively, we could just change the comparison to compare the names without considering the case (as I understand it, that would be equivalent to what you're doing here?).

What we might also want to do is thread this information through in some way - e.g. changing `ImportSuggestion` to be an enum with `Exact` and `Almost` (you can come up with a better name than this) variants so that we can make the diagnostic separate these two types of suggestions:

```
error[E0412]: cannot find type `Hashmap` in this scope
 --> src/main.rs:2:8
  |
2 |     m: Hashmap<String, ()>,
  |        ^^^^^^^ not found in this scope
  |
help: consider importing one of these items
  |
1 | use some::made:up::module::Hashmap;
  |
help: consider importing one of these similarly named items
  |
1 | use std::collections::HashMap;
  |
```

This should be easier to maintain because we don't have to keep a list of types like you've got here, and it'd work for non-`std` types too.

For an extern that *is* called in the crate that's being compiled, it does get a DefId and that DefId is then associated with the lang_item, but for what I'm calling "InjectedCode", this is not going to be the case.

author: richkadel

body:
> Yes, I did. As I understand it (and witnessed), when compiling a crate that does not call an extern, the extern is never pulled into the AST and therefore never lowered to HIR. 

The AST is created long before we determine which methods are actually called. Even if we could determine that a method was never called during AST construction, it would still need a `DefId` so that it can be be resolved by downstream crates.

I tried out your branch locally - I think I found the problem you ran into. The `lang_items` code emits some fairly confusing error messages.

When you place a `#[lang]` attribute on an `extern` item, it gets treated as a 'weak lang item' by `src/librustc_passes/weak_lang_items.rs`. However, the 'weak lang item' system is intended for lang items which eventually get linked to a symbol from some other crate - which is not how you're using `count_code_region`.

I would recommend adding a special case for your lang item in `Context::register`:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/219380d840877de97b0e17674be7212ebc929d51/src/librustc_passes/weak_lang_items.rs#L72-L83

You'll want to skip all of the logic in that method for `count_code_region` - although it's a foreign (`extern`) item, it's not a "weak lang item" as understood by that code.

That should cause `count_code_region` to be treated like a normal lang item, allowing you to obtain its `DefId` and insert a call to it into the MIR.

Let me know if any of this is unclear - I'd be happy to go into more detail.

body:
So I think what's actually happening is that when you add `println!()`s to the function body, some of the code added by that macro is eligible for [static promotion](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/1414-rvalue_static_promotion.md). Each promoted value gets its own `Body` which your code is then invoked for. Because these values were extracted out of the function, they use the function's `DefId` so when you call `debug!("instrumenting {:?}", src.def_id());`, you get the same `DefId` multiple times. If you log the full `src`, it should show that we're not running on the same `body` every time. 

You can see this by looking at the [Rust playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=ffb4b7013cea287855e78c81a383deb4). For a basic "hello world" application, if you click the "Show MIR" button (in the overflow menu button on the left hand side), you'll see that there is one body for `fn main()`, one body for a `&[std::fmt::ArgumentV1; 0]` which got promoted and one body for a `&[&str; 1]` which also got promoted. 

All that said, I don't have a problem with landing this as-is. We can always tweak this later and I think it's more important that we land something so we can start iterating on the coverage info generation.

body:
The pretty-printing is done using `pprust::nonterminal_to_string(nt)`, so it will use AST pretty-printing rather than token pretty-printing, and "`None` delimiters are printed as the empty string" is not too relevant.

Looks like we have two possible cases if we wrap `nt_to_tokenstream(...)` into a `None` group here:
- The original stream has a group with `None` delimiters, the reparsed stream has no group. That's a mismatch, spans are lost, and we cannot recover from such mismatch.
- The original stream has a group with `None` delimiters, the reparsed stream has a group with `Parenthesis` delimiters (due to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/75734). That's a mismatch, spans are lost, but we can recover from it by assuming "`Parenthesis` ≈ `None`" in the comparison function, and avoid losing the spans.

Ok, I guess the first case would be in majority, so wrapping `nt_to_tokenstream(...)` into a group would mostly defeat the purpose of this PR.
Sad.

Could you add a comment to the code explaining why we are not making a group here?

I think the rule is that if additions are small enough, e.g. just adding a trait implementation like `From`, they might be directly stabilized. However this seems like something the libs team might want to keep unstable for a bit, even if it is just because it needs bikeshedding for the name of the functions or things like that. But I'm sure of nothing, maybe this can be stabilized directly. @dtolnay or @cramertj can probably guide you for that.

What you will probably want to do is to mark these as unstable and [create a tracking issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/new?labels=C-tracking-issue&template=tracking_issue.md&title=Tracking+Issue+for+XXX). This will mean that the methods need a feature gate to be used and the libs team has freedom to make otherwise breaking changes to the methods.

body:
All registers can be used as inputs on Hexagon, that is the architecture doesn't not differentiate between `r0` and `r29` or `r30`, except for a small set of instructions which require fewer bits to encode registers.  As a matter of fact, most loads/stores to stack are done via `r29` or `r30` (i.e. `sp` or `fp`), and a return from a function that does not allocate stack space is done via `jumpr r31`.

All of these registers can also be modified, but that's typically a bad idea.

body: What happens here on overflow? It'll call `self.grow(bytes)`. Then what will happen -- panic, success? I think the possibilities need to be clearer here. In particular, `alloc_raw_fast()` returns `None` in two cases: "overflow", and "need to grow". I feel like those two cases need to be distinguished.
author: nnethercote

body:
From perspective of code that tried to use the current chunk the situation is the same: there is no capacity left and arena needs to grow. Overflow does not necessarily preclude later success if say the chunk had merely a high address, requested capacity was large, and the calculation overflowed.

The code then delegates the responsibility to handle the situation to `grow` and subsequently to `RawVec`. Under assumption that grow doesn't hit `checked_mul(2).unwrap()` (this could be saturated to `isize::MAX` to be a little bit friendlier to 32-bit systems), the allocation is performed by `RawVec` which panics when requested capacity exceeds `isize::MAX` (on 32-bit systems) and aborts on OOM.

We now only point at the uses of `T` when it is bare, otherwise we _assume_ that they allow `?Sized`. That example will suggest `T: ?Sized`:

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `T` cannot be known at compilation time
 --> file6.rs:6:21
  |
1 | struct Foo<T> {
  |            - required by this bound in `Foo`
...
6 | struct X<T: ?Sized>(Foo<T>);
  |          -          ^^^^^^ doesn't have a size known at compile-time
  |          |
  |          this type parameter needs to be `std::marker::Sized`
  |
  = help: the trait `std::marker::Sized` is not implemented for `T`
  = note: to learn more, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch19-04-advanced-types.html#dynamically-sized-types-and-the-sized-trait>
help: consider relaxing the implicit `Sized` restriction
  |
1 | struct Foo<T: ?Sized> {
  |             ^^^^^^^^
```

When applying it you get

```
error[E0277]: the size for values of type `T` cannot be known at compilation time
   --> file6.rs:2:5
    |: aborting due to previous error
1   | struct Foo<T: ?Sized> {
    |            - this type parameter needs to be `std::marker::Sized`
2   |     x: Vec<T>,
    |     ^^^^^^^^^ doesn't have a size known at compile-time
    |

    = note: to learn more, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch19-04-advanced-types.html#dynamically-sized-types-and-the-sized-trait>
```

I am indeed not verifying whether `Vec` or `Box` have a `T: ?Sized` or `T: Sized` constraint. That would be a good thing to add, but I feel that the current behavior is _good enough_ before adding more code to probe `Vec` and `Box` to identify what their bounds are.

body:
In terms of which crates to move where:

* Can we make sure that crates from `/std` depend only on other crates in std? IE, if we just eagerly move every `../../src` dependecy to `../../std`, would the split still be meaningful? It seems like it should be the case (because runtime code can depend only on runtime code). 
* If this is feasible, can we add a tidy check to ensure that `std -> src` dependencies don't resurface?
* Would the same hold in the opposite direction? Can we make sure that crates from `/src` don't depend on crates from `/std`? Can we enforce that? 

Ie, it seems like src and std *should* be independent bodies of code (one runs on target, another on host, etc), and, if that is indeed the case, I'd like this to be very cleary enforced, as "module X does **not** depend on module Y" is the strongest property you can get in terms of software architecture at large. 

EDIT: and this is why I propose to at least keep "runtime" terminology in mind (though I agree that we shouldn't use this word for the name of the dir): it's unclear if `libpanic_abort` belongs to the "standard library". It is obvious that it belongs to "runtime" though (if we treat "runtime" as a general "things which get  linked to your program", and not as the narrow "special langauge runtime services" (which includes std itself)).

body:
What happens when you store a function pointer in a type like `Result<&'static u8, fn()>`? (Example due to @eddyb)

In LLVM this type gets translated as `{ i64, ptr }`, where the first field indicates Ok vs Err and the 2nd field contains the data (`&u8` or `fn()`, depending on the first field). So it is fundamentally impossible to have a dedicated function pointer address space here. Doesn't sound like the approach taken in this PR can possibly work here?

body:
The problem with making command line arguments "consistent" with lint attributes, from my point of view, is that I think a lot of tools do inject (or freely mix) new command line arguments, and so I think users run into combinations of `-F` and `-A` on a single command line a lot more often than they run into `#[forbid]` and `#[allow]` in a single source item. 

A hard error for mixing `-F` and `-A` when they arose due to e.g. makefile variables is really annoying for end users.

(I suppose the analogy for source code items would be macro expansion, right? Does one see `#[allow]` getting injected from macros very often? I can admit this has crossed my mind at times, especially back when I put in the `push_unsafe`/`pop_unsafe` hacks [five years ago](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/27215/commits/1829fa5199bae5a192c771807c532badce14be37) ...)

body:
Returning a `usize` is incompatible with [`#![feature(repr128)]`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/56071).

We don't currently expose a way for users to determine the discriminant type of an enum (see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/70705). I think we have a few options here:

1. Make this function return a `u128`. Assuming we never add `u256/i256` to the language (both of which seem insane as an enum discriminant type), this would be compatible with enums with any number of variants.
2. Stabilize the `DiscriminantKind` trait, and have this function return a value of type `<T as DiscriminantKind>::Discrimininant>`. This does not solve the problem of converting the value to an integer, but it avoids returning  a `u128` for enums which don't need it.
3. Declare that enums with more than `usize::MAX` *variants* are unsupported (`#[repr(u128)]` enums with fewer variants are fine). We might want to consider changing this to `u64`, though I don't actually see any use-case for having an enum with more than 4 billion variants (let alone on a 32-bit platform).
author: Aaron1011

body: On second thought, Rust does have tier-3 support for a 16-bit platform (AVR). While having `u16::MAX` variants seems ridiculous, it seems *slightly* more questionable to forbid that compared to `u32::MAX` (though again, I have no idea why anyone would do such a thing). Perhaps a `u32` is the way to go here.

Good point with closures--I think you're right.

Regarding backwards compatibility, I've seen a few different opinions while reading through the various issues.  I don't have a strong opinion but some of the arguments I've seen:
* Use `unused_attributes` for backwards compatibility
* Hard error is consistent with `repr`, `inline`, `target_feature`
* Hard error to avoid footguns like `#[link_name = "foo"] extern {}`
* Hard error to avoid ICEs such as #64768

Looking at what was done with `inline`, the lint was used to avoid breaking the bitflags crate: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/65294#issuecomment-545418714

I'm curious to see how many crates, if any, are broken by this change but I have no problem changing to a lint if that's necessary.

@wesleywiser I'm a little unsure what you are suggesting for the query, particularly in the context of _not_ storing the `coverage_data` in the `mir::Body`.

I'm trying to familiarize myself with the queries and provider implementations, but I don't know how to set it up yet.

If I implement a `query coverage_data(DefId) -> mir::CoverageData`, but create the `CoverageData` during the `InstrumentCoverage` pass, where do I save the `CoverageData` so that the query implementation will return it?

It seems like it might be possible to store it directly in something like the rustc_metadata::rmeta tables, such as:

```rust
    coverage_data: Table<DefIndex, Lazy<mir::CoverageData>>,
```

or maybe add a new Map/cache directly to `GlobalCtxt`?

But there are probably other options, and in all of these cases, I can't pinpoint any examples in MIR-time processing where data like this is computed, stored, and then retrieved from a `query` downstream, without invoking the query to compute the value.

Any suggestions or code references I can model this after?

Thanks!
Rich

body:
So, what I was envisioning was a two-step approach where

- the `InstrumentCoverage ` MIR pass would only inject counters and nothing else

- the `coverage_data` query would get the MIR, count how many counters are in the MIR and hash the HIR body

The result of the `coverage_data` query would then be automatically persisted for you in the compiler session context. If you ever need that data cross-crate in the future, this would also set you up to be able to do that quite easily.
author: wesleywiser

body:
FYI, I was uploading a new commit just as you sent your reply.

Got it. I understand how that would work in the current context, but I wonder if this will have the best performance in the future.

I'm thinking of 2 or 3 possible upcoming changes that might still make it less efficient to split computing the state data (in the query) from instrumenting the MIR (in the pass). For example:

1. Just re-counting the injected calls requires walking the MIR again.
2. The implementation of the hash may change (Note that clang's approach does some coverage-specific analysis, so the hash is less sensitive to changes that don't affect flow).

With that in mind, is it reasonable to stash the coverage data in the `Body` struct, or do you feel strongly that this state data should be computed separately from the coverage analysis?

body:
It occurs to me that a MIR optimization could (a) duplicate a counter, or (b) inline counters from other functions. How should we deal with cases like that?

For (a) we could keep a set of counter id's we've already seen to deduplicate.

For handling (b), I'm assuming we'll want the name of the function where the counter originated in source? We could pass a def_id of the source function as part of the "intrinsic". But then how would we keep track of monomorphizations? We can always address this point in a follow-up PR, but it's worth thinking about.

The correct (or at least more correct) way to check if this is a pattern binding is to check that:

- This location is an `StatementKind::Assign` of an `Rvalue::Use`
- The assignment is to a user defined local (i.e. `self.body.local_decls[target].is_user_variable()` is true
- The ever initialized flow is false at this point.

Unfortunately the flows aren't available here currently, and changing things so that they are would be a fairly large change (#73552).

I think that if this is going to use an imperfect heuristic that would be fine with a fixme referencing that issue. The condition should be `moved_place.projection.iter().any(|p| matches!(p, ProjectionElem::Downcast)`.

I think this text could be improved. In particular, I had to check the example to understand whether the returned index is the last index of the first half or the first index of the second half. One suggestion:

> Returns the index of the partition point according to the given predicate (the index of the first element of the second partition).
>
> The slice is assumed to be partitioned according to the given predicate. This means that all elements for which the predicate returns `true` are at the start of the slice and all elements for which the predicate returns `false` are at the end. For example, `[7, 15, 3, 5, 4, 12, 6]` is a partitioned under the predicate `x % 2 != 0` (all odd numbers are at the start, all even at the end). 
>
> If this slice is not partitioned, the returned result is unspecified and meaningless, as this method performs a kind of binary search.

body:
Question: the vast majority of comments in these diffs take this form (i.e., "Caller must guarantee X"). Interestingly, usually in functions that have no associated comments, presumably because they are trait impls or in some other context where the comment is elsewhere.

Anyway, the question is -- do we think these comments make sense / add-value? Should we have some shorthand? 

I think this comment is a good example where I feel there *is* added value -- i.e., this doesn't just say "some unsafe thing" but it is rather specific about what we are assuming.

author: nikomatsakis
LeSeulArtichaut

body:
In my opinion, a detailed safety comment is useful:

- when the conditions that the caller must guarantee are only a subset of all the conditions required to call do the unsafe operation, because there are other invariants that we prove through other means. I think it is absolutely useful to have a detailed safety comments in these cases.
- when only a part of what the caller must guarantee is used, because the other guarantees are used elsewhere in the function. In this case, I think safety comments are useful because they help readers understand where the safety contract comes from, which I think is useful for contributors, or even for any consumer of the standard library who wants to understand where constraints come from.

I'm not an experienced rustacean used to writing unsafe stuff though, and I probably have too few experience to have a good opinion about all of this.

body:
These two are to prevent side-effects:

1. There is an assumption elsewhere that paths of variants are in the enum's declaration and not imported. With this assumption, the variant component is chopped and the rest of the path is assumed to be the enum's own path. For errors where a variant is used as the type instead of the enum, this causes funny looking invalid suggestions, i.e `foo` instead of `foo::MyEnum`.
2. Non-imports are prioritized, otherwise weird re-exports paths are picked instead, like `use io::sys::ext::net::sys_common::util::thread::panic::collections::HashMap;`, instead of just `use std::collections::HashMap;`.

I need to extract the values from the const u32 operands, and for the non-codegened intrinsics, I didn't like the unnecessary overhead of converting them to LLVM values (`OperandRef`s) and back again for no reason. So `is_codegen_intrinsic` takes the `rustc_middle::mir::Operand`s directly, before the args are converted to the backend.

Plus, for the intrinsics that are not passed through to `codegen_intrinsic_call`, this also avoids all of the other steps between the call to `is_codegen_intrinsic()` and `codegen_intrinsic_call()` in `block.rs`, and all of the prepwork in the implementation of `codegen_intrinsic_call()` prior to `match name {`. body:
@wesleywiser @bjorn3 - I don't (strictly speaking) have to address this in the current PR, but when I start injecting the calls to `coverage_counter_add`, `coverage_counter_subtract`, etc., I expect to also create a `temp` for the returned "unit", with associated `StorageLive` (in the Call `BasicBlock`) and `StorageDead` in the destination `BasicBlock`.

And if the backend implementation for these new intrinsics does not result in an LLVM intrinsic call (as is the case, per `rustc_codegen_llvm::is_codegen_intrinsic()`), the `StorageLive` and `StorageDead` calls and associated temp value have no purpose.

I don't want to make that decision during MIR generation. Whether the Call is converted into a backend call or not is (in my opinion) a codegen-time decision.

Will these unused `StorageLive` and `StorageDead` calls and the unit temp be optimized out by LLVM automatically? Or do I need to do something during codegen to effectively "erase" the storage statements from the LLVM IR in this case?

I see there are some intrinsics in `rustc_codegen_ssa::block` and `rustc_codegen_llvm::intrinsic` that also skip LLVM IR call generation, so maybe this is a problem/pattern that has already been solved; but they are not all the same.

Any pointers?

Thanks!
author: richkadel

body: `temp` is of type `()`, which isn't stored on the stack. This makes `StorageLive` and `StorageDead` a nop during codegen. `StorageLive` and `StorageDead` were originally introduced to tell LLVM when stack slots were live or dead. (They are now also used by MIR borrowck and MIRI)

I've looked at how `validate_res_from_ribs` is being used and how it differs from how `search_label` and `resolve_expr` are working - I can see a handful of different approaches to reconcile the differences, but I'm not sure which you'd prefer (or intended).

1. Modify `search_labels` to walk all scopes, ignoring "barrier" ribs, returning `ResolutionError::UnresolvedLabel` if there were no match.

3. Extend `validate_res_from_ribs` to handle the `Res::Label` case, returning `ResolutionError::LabelOutOfScope` (or something like that) if the `Res::Label` was found through a "barrier" rib.

However, if introducing a `Res::Label` would be inappropriate, a `validate_label_from_ribs` function could be introduced, which performs the function of `validate_res_from_ribs` but for labels - `search_labels` would be modified as in the previous proposal.

body:
Mm, indeed. The `BitSet` iteration is faster. It goes like this (I find this implementation quite incredible to be honest)

- You make a `BitIter` from the `BitSet`.
- `BitIter` uses `Word` as `u64`, and through that, it calls `u64::trailing_zeros()` to compute the position of the next element in the set.
- `u64::trailing_zeros()` calls upon `intrinsics::cttz`
- And finally, `intrinsics::cttz` calls upon [the LLVM `cttz` intrinsic](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#llvm-cttz-intrinsic) which is crazy fast.

I think it's incredible because this takes the normal iteration over indexes and makes it faster. What the heck, incredible. I feel like I have so much still to learn about data structures, from looking at this. :heart:

body:
Looking more at this loop, I would split it into several parts:
* a loop to just call `super_projection_elem` uniformly on all the elems, to get it out of the way (it only serves to visit the index local of an `Index` projection, with a `Copy context)
* find the *first* `Deref`, if there is one, e.g. with  `.position(|elem| matches!(elem, mir::PlaceElem::Deref))`
* loop over the "direct projections" (i.e. before any `Deref`, if any) and do `self.not_ssa(local); break;` at the first sign of trouble

I mostly want this for clarity, but that last part has some promise for making this more efficient, so here's a few more ideas:
* `context` wouldn't change across it, meaning `if is_consume(context)` can be placed around the whole loop
* there could be a quick check that all the elements are fields, to avoid time even looking at the layouts
* we probably should check all the field projections (like today / this PR) but if we go forward, from the `local` to the innermost field, we should almost always hit the non-SSA layout first, making the rejection cheaper
* we could call `visit_local` before the loop, and skip the loop if `non_ssa_locals` already contains the local (see also the comment at the top of this file, which would make this more useful)
* if we keep the monomorphized `TyAndLayout` of the local (which we always have to compute anyway) around, we could start from it and just go `layout = layout.field(self.fx, i)` at every step instead of computing the whole type and monomorphizing every time

body:
https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/send-and-sync.html

> Some types allow you to have multiple aliases of a location in memory while mutating it. Unless these types use synchronization to manage this access, they are absolutely not thread-safe. Rust captures this through the Send and Sync traits.

>    A type is Send if it is safe to send it to another thread.
>    A type is Sync if it is safe to share between threads (&T is Send).

These are automatically derived, but they are not part of the language. Additionally, adding `impl<T> Sync for Rc<T>` would be UB because it could lead to double-frees (e.g. if the counter is not updated atomically).

I recommended a short summary of this in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/73943#discussion_r448649436 but it's not a bad idea to go more in depth.

body:
The trait currently has a safety invariant attached: that of the indexing operation being infallible, which `get_unchecked` has not (in other words, given the safety invariant of the trait, implementing the trait for `[T]` slices would violate the contract); that's what allows it to offer a non-`unsafe` `get_unchecked`.
It could be implemented for `[T; N] where N ≥ 3`, or for `(_, _, T, ...)`, where bound-checking the indexing operation can be skipped, without having to be `unsafe`.

  - [Example](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=5421d0390186b9fe8439184ea2a28d7e)

I like that example because it shows the benefits / the power of `unsafe trait`s: by restricting the subset of applicable types (and thus inputs), you can make a generally `unsafe` operation no longer be so.

body:
If something fails to compile, it might not fully run the stage of the compiler that would use the external crate. So hyper might *appear* to be used to folks but the compiler won't recognize it because of the compilation error. It might only see some crates, it might see no crates at all. All bets are off. So that's why I made compile fail cases not count into crate usages. If your external crate is only used in compile fail cases of rustdoc snippets, then maybe removing it is a good idea :).

Regarding your example, note that `extern crate hyper` marks the crate used by this lint just as any `pub use` or `use` reexport would :), see PR description.

`noexcept` means we'd need an effect system -- because Rust is higher-order, adding a simple attribute is not enough, you have to be able to mark `fn` ptrs and methods in `trait` implementations as `noexcept`. It's a huge amount of complexity for a niche usecase such as `take_mut`.

body:
> also make sure that indeed [...], `unwrap_unchecked` and [...] never panic?

So I added an `unwrap_unchecked_unpanicky` that never does. The old `unwrap_unchecked` seems meant not to prevent panic but to optimize it away in a release build. One would indeed think the code to panic wastes resources, but I've always wondered how many pennies we save this way. Time to measure!

```
benchcmp old plain_unwrap_1 --threshold 5
 name                                           old ns/iter  plain_unwrap_1 ns/iter  diff ns/iter   diff %  speedup
 btree::map::insert_rand_10_000                 33           35                                 2    6.06%   x 0.94
 btree::map::iteration_1000                     4,027        1,133                         -2,894  -71.86%   x 3.55
 btree::map::iteration_100000                   498,075      294,756                     -203,319  -40.82%   x 1.69
 btree::map::iteration_20                       80           21                               -59  -73.75%   x 3.81
 btree::map::iteration_mut_1000                 3,898        1,019                         -2,879  -73.86%   x 3.83
 btree::map::iteration_mut_100000               476,445      275,236                     -201,209  -42.23%   x 1.73
 btree::map::iteration_mut_20                   78           21                               -57  -73.08%   x 3.71
 btree::set::difference_random_100_vs_100       745          686                              -59   -7.92%   x 1.09
 btree::set::difference_random_10k_vs_10k       186,910      163,967                      -22,943  -12.27%   x 1.14
 btree::set::difference_staggered_100_vs_100    765          693                              -72   -9.41%   x 1.10
 btree::set::difference_staggered_10k_vs_10k    73,799       64,744                        -9,055  -12.27%   x 1.14
 btree::set::intersection_random_100_vs_100     643          347                             -296  -46.03%   x 1.85
 btree::set::intersection_random_10k_vs_10k     163,212      120,081                      -43,131  -26.43%   x 1.36
 btree::set::intersection_staggered_100_vs_100  624          373                             -251  -40.22%   x 1.67
 btree::set::intersection_staggered_10k_vs_10k  60,801       34,355                       -26,446  -43.50%   x 1.77
 btree::set::is_subset_100_vs_100               589          302                             -287  -48.73%   x 1.95
 btree::set::is_subset_10k_vs_10k               58,620       29,608                       -29,012  -49.49%   x 1.98
```
I'm not kidding, I cleaned config.toml and rebuilt with the same result. Replacing the body of `unwrap_unchecked` with `val.unwrap()` boosts iteration performance considerably. This is not related to the panic-safe changes for this PR in navigate.rs, but the iterator code higher up in map.rs also does a lot of `unwrap_unchecked`.

Also replacing the body of `unwrap_unchecked_unpanicky`, thus violating safety preconditions, does not help performance.

But wait... am I just wrongly assuming that in the release builds benchmarked, the `if cfg!(debug_assertions)` code gets compiled away? No, making `unwrap_unchecked` identical to the new `unwrap_unchecked_unpanicky` does not change performance.

I conclude that this topic is unrelated to this PR. This PR (or actually, the PR where we introduced `replace`) needs an unpanicky `unwrap_unchecked` but not all `unwrap_unchecked` should be like that.

body:
Hm… I think I did a bad job at conveying the point I was trying to make here.

What I really wanted to say is that this introduces another source of truth on how the optimisation behaves and where it applies. There is already some code that codifies this kind of information in the layout calculation code (although not easily reusable here, I think) and  `is_repr_nullable_ptr` is yet another place where this happens. _If_, somebody was adjusting how this optimisation works to e.g. admit more cases or fix a bug… there is no provision to ensure that they do not miss updating all of those portions of code, including here. So its better to have fewer such sources of truth than more.

In particular to me it looks like `is_repr_nullable_ptr` already goes to some length to make sure that the contained field is a type that participates in nullable type optimisation, so I suspect this check could be dropped entirely. Is there perhaps a specific reason you want to check ranges that I’m missing? Maybe it would then make sense to move that check to more shared code like `is_repr_nullable_ptr` in the first place?

body:
>its better to have fewer such sources of truth than more

Ohh, I see what you mean. Yeah, I agree -- that makes sense.

> Is there perhaps a specific reason you want to check ranges that I’m missing?

`is_repr_nullable_ptr` only checks if something like Option<NonZeroUsize> is okay, but doesn't check the type that it's casted to/from. I check the ranges to ensure, for example, that `Option<NonZeroUsize>` is being correctly converted to `usize`, and not to `isize` or another same-sized-but-incorrect type.

> move that check to more shared code like is_repr_nullable_ptr

I've currently got `is_repr_nullable_ptr` just returning the type inside the Option-like enum, which I've come to realise isn't actually that useful. Yeah, I'll go with this -- it'd probably be better to have `is_repr_nullable_ptr` return the type that the `Option<T>` is FFI-convertible to (if it exists), and ClashingExternDeclarations can just compare `primitive_ty` to that type.

So with these defaults tools use path trimming and are slow by default.
I think it would be a safer default for tools to not use path trimming at all.

So the option needs to be about path printing specifically rather than about good path bugs in general, and it also needs to be a three variant enum rather than a boolean (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/73996#issuecomment-679355482).
```rust
enum TrimmedDefPaths {
    Never, // [default] `try_print_trimmed_def_path` never prints a trimmed path and never calls the expensive query
    Always, // `try_print_trimmed_def_path` calls the expensive query, the query doesn't call `delay_good_path_bug`
    GoodPath, // `try_print_trimmed_def_path` calls the expensive query, the query calls `delay_good_path_bug`
}
```

So I went down a rabbit hole here - it's true that this fails to compile, but it's not because of the `where` clause. Rather, it's because `inner` was dropped at the end of the block, so it can't be used outside; that error would happen with or without the `where`. I tried removing the `assert_eq!()` afterwards and found that actually compiles without a problem, even though `outer` lives longer than `inner`! https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=0e254df4b5f8ce301b2c253acbd04e94

I think what's going on is that `longer` is being implicitly reborrowed for a lifetime that's less than `inner`, something like `select_where(&*longer, shorter, false);`. Rather than try and mess with this more, would it be simpler to show what happens if you don't have the bound? I think that error makes it more clear why it's useful: https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=37482da9175c6a0ae0615c3a8cc36f97

```
error[E0623]: lifetime mismatch
 --> src/main.rs:3:7
  |
1 | fn select_where<'a, 'b>(s1: &'a str, s2: &'b str, second: bool) -> &'a str {
```

The code says "// never overflow because `slice::len()` max is `isize::MAX`."

That's correct for non-ZSTs, but strictly the restriction, as seen in https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/slice/fn.from_raw_parts.html#safety is that the length *in bytes* is at most that -- so if `sizeof(T) == 0` then the size in bytes is also `0`, and `usize::MAX` is allowed. body:
OK, so, the idea is that... if we are providing a value `V` for some variable `?A`, then we have to ensure that the value `V` can be named from within the universe of `?A`. e.g., if `?A` is in the root universe, then `V` can only reference names in the root universe.

Therefore, if `V` contains some other variable `?B`, then the universe `Universe(?B)` of `?B` must be some ancestor of `Universe(?A)`.

We have to decide how "eagerly" we want to report these errors.

In chalk at least, we treat type variables and lifetime variables differently. For example, if we have `exists<T> { forall<U> { T = U } }` in chalk, we consider that to be a unification failure.  But if we have `exists<'a> { forall<'b> { 'a = 'b } }` in chalk, we produce a region constraint that will never be satisfied.

However, Rust doesn't presently have binders over type variables like this, so the question doesn't arise in stable rust. I guess I have to go read what the unification code does now.

This may cause an issue with temporary lifetimes, see [this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48732263/why-is-rusts-assert-eq-implemented-using-a-match).

You can use `match` with `#[allow_internal_unstable(type_ascription)]` to work around this problem:

I made this change to be able to match the type on the `span` field of these two different patterns:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/74211/files#diff-2f2c99a2d0f3967b759026f70c4313b8R517-R518

```rust
                PathSource::Expr(Some(Expr { span, kind: ExprKind::Call(_, _), .. }))
                | PathSource::TupleStruct(span) => {
```

Because the contents of the `Expr` variant is `Option<&Expr>` its `span` field is `&Span` while the `TupleStruct` holds a `Span`. I can't use `ref` on one and not the other because that is different bindings for the same field (a restriction that might be lifted but is still there). Borrowing `source` makes them both be `&Span` without any further changes.

body:
Newest version of the code, in godbolt: https://rust.godbolt.org/z/Pc6175.

```asm
example::before:
        mov     rax, rdi
        mov     qword ptr [rdi], 1
        vxorps  xmm0, xmm0, xmm0
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 8], xmm0
        mov     qword ptr [rdi + 24], 1
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 32], xmm0
        ret

example::after:
        sub     rsp, 48
        mov     rax, rdi
        mov     qword ptr [rsp], 1
        vxorps  xmm0, xmm0, xmm0
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rsp + 8], xmm0
        mov     qword ptr [rsp + 24], 1
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rsp + 32], xmm0
        mov     rcx, qword ptr [rsp]
        mov     qword ptr [rdi], rcx
        vmovups xmm0, xmmword ptr [rsp + 8]
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 8], xmm0
        mov     rcx, qword ptr [rsp + 24]
        mov     qword ptr [rdi + 24], rcx
        mov     rcx, qword ptr [rsp + 16]
        mov     qword ptr [rdi + 16], rcx
        mov     rcx, qword ptr [rsp + 24]
        mov     qword ptr [rdi + 24], rcx
        vmovups xmm0, xmmword ptr [rsp + 32]
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 32], xmm0
        add     rsp, 48
        ret
```

It appears to me that the difference is entirely a consequence of "return value optimization" not kicking in for the MaybeUninit for some reason, which seems fixable in the compiler. Changing the following two lines fixes the performance issue and gets exactly the same machine code as before (but isn't correct).

```diff
- let mut data: MaybeUninit<[T; N]> = MaybeUninit::uninit();
+ let mut data: [T; N] = unsafe { mem::uninitialized() }; // unsound

- unsafe { data.assume_init() }
+ data
```

```asm
example::before:
        mov     rax, rdi
        mov     qword ptr [rdi], 1
        vxorps  xmm0, xmm0, xmm0
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 8], xmm0
        mov     qword ptr [rdi + 24], 1
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 32], xmm0
        ret

example::after:
        mov     rax, rdi
        mov     qword ptr [rdi], 1
        vxorps  xmm0, xmm0, xmm0
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 8], xmm0
        mov     qword ptr [rdi + 24], 1
        vmovups xmmword ptr [rdi + 32], xmm0
        ret
```

body:
It would need to be added as a new method to `Emitter`.  

For `EmitterWriter`, it would need to check the `Destination` to determine whether or not the destination supports color.  For `Terminal(StandardStream)`, it would check [`supports_color`](https://docs.rs/termcolor/1.1.0/termcolor/trait.WriteColor.html#tymethod.supports_color).  For `Buffered(BufferWriter)`, it would need to call `buffer().supports_color()`. For `Destination::Raw`, it would be the 2nd tuple value (the bool indicating color support).

For `JsonEmitter`, it would need to call [`new_emitter`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/527a685e40d8fbe61442bdbd510c2b4e1d248019/src/librustc_errors/emitter.rs#L54-L65) and do the same checks as above.

Other emitters would need similar treatment, though I think the rest of them are special (like `SilentEmitter` which could just return false).

> **Note:** This example trades correctness for simplicity. In order to prevent

But also it is just surprising to me to have `type_of` require us to type-check the closure. Well I tested the one project I had sitting at hand, it worked, but that's a fairly small project which is nearly entirely in `main`.

I also now recall some of what @ketsuban told me when he first explained GBA stuff to me, that `lld` can't be used because it doesn't support `ARMv4T`. Based on [this PR](https://reviews.llvm.org/D53444) in the LLVM repo it seems like even recently they don't have support for ARMv4T in `lld`, and seemingly they don't plan to support it either.

The difficulty is that ARMv4T has a `BX` ("branch-exchange") instruction which is used to switch between a32 and t32 states in the CPU. Then in ARMv5T they added `BLX` ("branch-link-exchange"), which also leaves the next address in the link register as the branch-exchange happens (so that you can `bx lr` later to return). In some sitautions, LLD will use the BLX instruction, but ARMv4T doesn't support it, so you UB the CPU with an illegal instruction.

body:
Not sure what you mean by "equally mutable".

`UnsafeCell` affects shared references but not mutable references. IOW, `&mut UnsafeCell<T>` is the same as `&mut T`. `UnsafeCell` is for being able to mutate data behind a shared reference. `DormanMutRef` does nothing like that, so I do not understand how it makes any sense to add `UnsafeCell` here. Where is there [interior mutability](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/interior-mutability.html) here? The answer is "nowhere", and this immediately implies that `UnsafeCell` is unnecessary.

> Miri's blessing

You'd get Miri's blessing here even if you made `DormantMutRef` just a newtype around `&mut T`, the `UnsafeCell` changes nothing. But that's an instance of https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines/issues/125, it's an open question what we really want here.
author: RalfJung

body:
There is one difference with the `Vec` implementation: it does not leak in the end, because the vector keeps hold of its buffer. It's potentially wasteful to carry on with a massive buffer containing 0 elements (or just fewer elements than before, like in [the only test using `forget`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/library/alloc/tests/vec.rs#L668) in the library directory). But when the vector eventually is dropped, the buffer is deallocated, and there is no more leak.

For `BTreeMap`, right now I see it as a violation to keep a whole tree hanging, when the length is set to 0. So it must be moved away, and the obvious parking place is `DrainFilter`. But that means if you `forget` the `DrainFilter`, there is a undeniable leak, i.e., I cannot test this without Miri complaining about the leak. Possible conclusions, none of which I like:
- That is just what leak amplification is. Ideally Miri would report leaks per test case and could be told to ignore leaks in this test case, but it doesn't, so we must configure such test cases to be ignored by Miri.
- We need to reserve another parking place, in `BTreeMap` itself, where its drop handler will find it and clean up the mess. But that seems obviously inferior to…
- We don't consider it a violation to have a whole tree when length is 0, but a sign that the tree still needs to be cleaned up. Or…
- We don't do any leak amplification and we don't consider it a violation to have empty internal roots, but a sign that these need to be popped off. Or…
- We don't do any leak amplification and we consider it normal to have empty internal roots on top. The number of nodes and how key/values are spread over them already depends on history, so it's not _that_ weird, but still a risk because it only occurs very rarely in the wild and will only be tested in dedicated test cases.

Part of my drive to have `DrainFilter` do work in the drop handler is to allow much smarter things: to not continuously keep the tree in shape by moving elements about, while it might turn out that the caller drains most of the rest of the tree. But that's not happening.

So perhaps the best conclusion is to continue to let `DrainFilter` sometimes mess with the root node while iterating over the same node. It already merges the keys/values it's iterating over into another node, so how is setting the node's parent any worse? Maybe it just seems worse because the code doing that is in separate functions.

body:
Yup, this `memory_atomic_wait32` function only requires the pointer to point to a valid 32-bit value (like i32 or AtomicU32) that it will read, nothing else. There's now safe wrappers in `sys/wasm/futex_atomics.rs` that make this guarantee by requiring a `&AtomicI32`. The unsafety in wasm's condvar/mutex/etc. could be avoided by using `AtomicI32` and those wrappers instead. But that can be a separate PR.

> make lock safe

For some platforms (wasm, cloudabi, windows), the mutex implementations could be safe. But some others (unix) have extra requirements about pinning/moving. That's why all of the locks on all platforms are unsafe, to not make a commitment about them being safe. Maybe the unsafe ones can be replaced at some point by an alternative implementation (e.g. parking_lot or some other implementation), but that still requires a lot of work.

author: yoshuawuyts

body:
Even in that scenario, existence of fork call makes more processes. So it might be a single process or not. That is basically ignoring the existence of fork and CommandExt.

Moreover, cgroups are not for single process. You can restrict a resource allocation to a single process or multiple processes. But if we are talking about cgroups then this will not show all exposed hardware threads to process/processes when cpuset is used.

One more thing, when thread affinity mask applied you won't get the all cores exposed to the process/processes. Same applies to programs using Numa and deployed with affinity mask applied.

Yet another thing is, after mask applied you will get vcores assigned to you. Not what OS gives then.

In the light of these, writing correct comment for this is important. It is not hardware threads, it is not os exposing and there are some other runtimes which is used as target arch and don't have OS and things mentioned above.

Oh btw, check out sched_setaffinity for solving the last two problems.

**Edit:** While thinking about it. A proper name for this would be `available_logical_cores`. With the current implementation this is not what it is done. But if cpuset restrictions and such is lifted and get the actual logical core count that's what it does.

body:
So actually I'm not sure there is a bug here. There has been a long-standing debate about the correct semantics of auto traits in the face of negative impls, but the current semantics (not, perhaps *100%* settled) is that

* If the user writes ANY explicit impl, positive or negative, then the compiler generates NO automatic impl

This was perhaps to be paired with disallowing negative impls that were overly narrow, such as `!Foo for Bar<()>`. 

So in this case, writing `impl !Send for Bar<()>` (for example) would mean that the compiler does not add an automatic `Send for Bar`  impl at all.

It's debatable what's more intuitive. I personally prefer the current rules -- I would prefer that if you write *anything* explicit, you must write *everything* explicit. But also this avoids having a setup (which specialization/coherence currently do not permit) where you have a "base impl" that accepts lots of things and then "negative impls" that cut out "exceptions" where that base impl no longer applies.

In other words, given specialization (and auto traits as currently implemented and specified), if you know that a "base impl" applies, you know that the trait is implemented, and no specialization can make that "untrue".

body:
I just tried this out, it's intriguing.

First, were you thinking that `as_str()` would become something like this?
```
    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
        with_interner(|interner| unsafe {
            std::mem::transmute::<&str, &str>(interner.get(*self))
        })
    }
```
Instead of falsely claiming that the lifetime of the result is `static`, it falsely claims that the lifetime matches that of `&self`. So it's still a lie, but it's a much smaller lie. (Unless I've misunderstood something?)

I tried making this change without this PR's commits applied. It worked amazingly well. There are only about a dozen places where I need to use the old version, mostly where we are sorting vectors containing symbols, e.g.:
```
        names.sort_by_key(|n| n.as_str());
```
(I get borrowck errors with the new `as_str()` formulation.) The `ToStableHashKey` impl for `Symbol` is also tricky.

I can imagine with some effort it might be possible to eliminate `SymbolStr` entirely. Also, working with `&str` is nicer than `SymbolStr`, because it avoids the need for some `&` and `&*` occurrences.

Having said all that, won't this PR block this new approach? `SymbolStr` must exist with inline symbols -- because it contains the byte array in which we de-inline inlined symbols for `as_str()`.

A sort impl for `VecDeque` was submitted in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/69400#issuecomment-597644295, but was then abandoned in favor of `make_contiguous`. I agree with you that it's probably possible to implement an efficient sort directly on a `VecDeque`, though it's certainly a bit more complicated (and would also add many extra methods). For example, a straightforward heapsort wouldn't work unless you do some tricky wrapping index calculation for child/parent indexing. Or you could go for two heapsorts + a merge (which I think the original PR did), but that is also a bit slower.

Ultimately, I think `make_contiguous` is useful regardless of whether we get sorting. And this doc text can always be updated to reflect added sorting methods if those get added later.

body:
In the IEEE 754 standard (which is very relevant in this context) precision has a very particular definition:

> **2.1.41 precision:** The maximum number *p* of significant digits that can be represented in a format, or the
number of digits to that a result is rounded.

With that definition, the precision is a property of the format, not of the number; and it would always be a precision of 24 bits for `f32`. Maybe a better word would be resolution, which I think means basically the same thing but is not explicitly overloaded by the IEEE 754 standard.

Here’s something I have so far (caveat untested, unchecked and not validated):

```llvm
  ; check that the number is within the expected bounds and just convert if the number is in range
  %inbound_lower = fcmp oge double %0, 0xC1E0000000000000
  %inbound_upper = fcmp ole double %0, 0x41DFFFFFFFC00000
  %inbounds = and i1 %inbound_lower, %inbound_upper
  br i1 %inbounds, label %convert, label %specialcase

specialcase:
  %isnan = fcmp ord double %0, 0.000000e+00 ; can probably also be `!inbound_lower && !inbound_upper`?
  ; select a max/min value for the case where float is not nan
  %result_notnan = select i1 %inbound_lower, i32 2147483647, i32 -2147483648
  ; nan or min/max
  %result_nan = select i1 %isnan, i32 0, i32 %result_notnan
  ret i32 %result_nan

convert:
  %result = fptosi double %0 to i32
  ret i32 %result
```

body:
This is what I ended up with in the end

```llvm
    ;; block so far... %0 is the argument
    %inbound_lower = fcmp oge double %0, 0xC1E0000000000000
    %inbound_upper = fcmp ole double %0, 0x41DFFFFFFFC00000
    ;; match (inbound_lower, inbound_upper) { 
    ;;     (true, true) => %0 can be converted without trapping
    ;;     (false, false) => %0 is a NaN
    ;;     (true, false) => %0 is too large
    ;;     (false, true) => %0 is too small
    ;; }
    ;;
    ;; The (true, true) check, go to %convert if so.
    %inbounds = and i1 %inbound_lower, %inbound_upper
    br i1 %inbounds, label %convert, label %specialcase

specialcase:
    ;; Handle the cases where the number is NaN, too large or too small
    
    ;; Either (true, false) or (false, true)
    %is_not_nan = or i1 %inbound_lower, %inbound_upper
    ;; Figure out which saturated value we are interested in if not `NaN`
    %saturated = select i1 %inbound_lower, i32 2147483647, i32 -2147483648
    ;; Figure out between saturated and NaN representations
    %result_nan = select i1 %is_not_nan, i32 %saturated, i32 0
    br label %done

convert:
    %result = call i32 @llvm.wasm.trunc.signed.i32.f64(double %0) ; fptosi double %0 to i32
    br label %done

done:
    %r = phi i32 [ %result, %convert ], [ %result_nan, %specialcase ]
    ;; continues here
```

Here’s a godbolt comparison of the two approaches: https://rust.godbolt.org/z/cnEGWM. Curiously the output in godbolt is very different from what was posted in the PR description, and I’m not sure why the difference (maybe `i32` vs `u32`?).

Anyway, comparing just the godbolt output the code generated from the snippet above looks somewhat better to my wasm-untrained eye. This code is also something LLVM is not really able to optimize much further. So at the very least doing something along the lines of this snippet can be a win in terms of the compile time.

If you don’t want to attempt to integrate something like this, that's also fine with me. In that case let me know and I’ll r+ this.

body:
Yeah, `is_none` and `is_disabled` have different semantics.

 [`is_disabled`](https://docs.rs/tracing/0.1.17/tracing/span/struct.Span.html#method.is_disabled):
> Returns true if this span was disabled by the subscriber and does not exist.

[`is_none`](https://docs.rs/tracing/0.1.17/tracing/span/struct.Span.html#method.is_none):
>  Returns `true` if this span was constructed by `Span::none` and is empty.
>
> If `is_none` returns `true` for a given span, then `is_disabled` will
> also return `true`. However, when a span is disabled by the subscriber
> rather than constructed by `Span::none`, this method will return
> `false`, while `is_disabled` will return `true`.

So, `is_none` _only_ returns `true` if the span was constructed by an explicit call to the `Span::none()` function. Since these spans were created by a macro and may be disabled by the subscriber, they will never return `true` for calls to `is_none`. That means that all the code that previously was only run at the trace level is no always being run.

I think there may also be _some_ minor additional performance cost to creating these empty spans in the case where they are _not_ disabled, but I don't think that's as big an issue. The best solution for _that_ would probably be eventually refactoring this code to not rely on empty spans to test if a given level/module combination is enabled.

cc @rust-lang/wg-mir-opt this PR uses `self.temps[local]`, similarly to how we treat reborrows (`&*foo` if `foo` is a reference). I believe this is preferrable to the other possible solutions, namely:

* optimizing the MIR before promotion (and thus borrowck!) to convert `*FOO` to `BAR` where `const FOO: &'static T = &BAR;`. While I believe this optimization is strictly correct, doing such optimizations before borrowck seems dangerous
* changing MIR building to not emit those constants. This is very hard, because when building the MIR for a `BAR` access, we don't know whether it's going to be for a reference or for a read.

body: Theoretically this `place` may be `*some_local.field`, where the projection is `[.field, *]`. In that case simply grabbing the `local` and reading its value won't be correct. While `check_static_ptr` requires the constant to be just a pointer, `struct Foo { field: &'static i32 }` would also be represented as just a pointer. So I think there should be an additional `proj_base.is_empty()` check. Since currently no MIR can get built that contains something like that, you can just `assert!(proj_base.is_empty())` after the `check_static_ptr` check. body:
(summarizing my discussion with @spastorino on Zulip)
I think a bigger issue than special-casing the shape of the pattern, is that `within_fn_param` applies recursively to every nested pattern in a `fn` parameter, *instead of* to the parameter pattern itself.

So my suggestion is to replace it with a "shallow" version (bikeshed name: `outermost_fn_param_pat`) that `visit_pat` temporarily sets back to `false` around its `walk_pat` call, so that the `#![feature(unsized_fn_params)]` path is only taken for `fn` parameters themselves, *not* any other patterns nested in them.

body:
In my opinion the original wording of slices being a "view", and being represented as a pointer and a length is somewhat confusing as slices, from a syntax standpoint, are themselves pointers(/references). My rewording is probably not perfect. Especially the term `regular pointer` is somewhat unspecific.

The point I wanted to make is to more closely define what exactly the term "slice" refers to. Which types fall under this definition?

The way I understand it, `&[T]`, and `&mut [T]` are definitely slices. Box<[T]> and Rc<[T]> have all the behavior of a slice, as they also Deref into a `[T]`, so I think they are slices as well. I'm not sure about `*mut [T]`/`*const [T]`. They still behave like a slice in the sense that they store a pointer + length, but you have to manually dereference them to "view" into the memory they point to, or even access the length. However with the other types, this still happens, just implicitly.

Defining a slice as "any pointer/reference" may be too broad. It's just what I think should be included. I just believe it is important to make it obvious that a slice is actually the reference, not the thing behind the reference.

I hope that explains the thought process that went into that rewording and can help to find a better one!

body:
I agree that we should make a change to avoid the confusion here, but I'm not sure that this change is it. 

This PR will add the note to *every* `improper_ctypes` and `improper_ctypes_definitions` lint. In most cases, I'd expect the user to have specified the ABI, so this addition would only add confusion (e.g. this message could be interpreted as suggesting that the compiler has determined that you are using the unstable Rust ABI but haven't specified it explicitly, despite having specified another ABI). In fact, this lint doesn't even trigger when using the Rust ABI, so this note would *only* appear when the user *has* specified (or was defaulted to) a non-Rust-internal ABI.

Unfortunately, at this point in compilation, we don't know whether the user did not specify `extern` (and thus defaulted to a Rust ABI), specified only `extern` (and defaulted to the C ABI), or specified the ABI manually. If we were able to easily determine this, then I'd be happy with adding a note when we defaulted to the C ABI which informs the user that has happened.

As you suggest, a lint/warning/error on `#[no_mangle]` without `extern` might be appropriate (I don't know how common this is to say whether or not it makes sense); alternatively, we could keep track of whether the ABI was specified further into the compiler to make this addition contextual.

---

If you want to try and make this contextual, the approach I would take is to introduce a `Abi` type in `src/librustc_hir/hir.rs`:

```rust
enum AbiSource {
	Explicit,
	Implicit,
	None
}

struct Abi {
    kind: rustc_target::spec::abi::Abi,
    source: AbiSource,
}
```

Replace `rustc_target::spec::abi::Abi`'s uses in all of `src/librustc_hir/hir.rs` and `src/rustc_middle/ty/sty.rs` (all of the HIR and Ty more generally, but it'll be mostly those files) with your new type and create it here:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/e614f66800c2b289f6c969dbabd2902e253a5e69/src/librustc_ast_lowering/item.rs#L1254-L1260

Then, in this lint, adjust callers of `check_type_for_ffi_and_report_errors` to thread the `AbiSource` through to the `emit_ffi_unsafe_type_lint` and then use that to only emit the note that you added here when appropriate (and change it to inform the user what the default is, not what they might have meant).

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/e614f66800c2b289f6c969dbabd2902e253a5e69/src/librustc_lint/types.rs#L1038-L1044

I'd also file an issue to track the potential improvement to `#[no_mangle]` w/out `extern` (or open another PR, but it might warrant some discussion first).

A reminder how we came here: [Mark introduced the `replace` function](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/68827#discussion_r385134726) to capture a pattern that had been scattered throughout iterator implementations. I got away then without checking or documenting compliance to the no-panic rule. That trickled down to tens of functions receiving a comment in this PR. I'm not at all sure that is what Ralf meant, it could just mean to have a single comment in the new `take_mut` function, the same as Mark wrote (or pasted) in `replace` (as well as removing the `debug_assert`s eager to panic).

I would put either nothing or a "[no_panic]" comment there - it looks less casual, and it's a term you can look up. I haven't found any explanation of "unwind(aborts)", and that (as an attribute) it's used on functions interfacing with C++.

> RUST_BACKTRACE seems completely useless in these double panic situations. 

Shouldn't be the case. I just confirmed RUST_BACKTRACE will produce backtrace just fine. Backtrace is generally preferred to just aborting when the situation allows, because it gives you more information without debugger.

> avoid the performance backlash of unwrap_unchecked

unwrap_unchecked uses `unreachable_unchecked()`, and it is *supposed* to be faster. The current performance drawback is due to a bug in LLVM (#74615). If that get's fixed, unwrap_unchecked would be much faster than unwrap_or_abort.
author: nbdd0121

body:
> Calling unwrap_unchecked is not unsafe anymore with PanicGuard.

I don't believe you. If there is nothing to unwrap, our call to `unwrap_unchecked` reaches UB and anything can happen. Not a problem, because the function whose body we're talking about is also tagged unsafe and documented to the caller when this could happen. But still unsafe in my book.

My point was that the call requires an unsafe block, even if there wasn't any UB lurking, so reading the code has a cognitive overhead. You could say that having to understand yet another variation on unwrap also has that overhead. Also, I struggle with the fact/perception that aborting is safe and UB, which includes having the luck to recover and the chance to save a user's work, is unsafe. Now I think that aborting, although classified as safe, is far worse than unsafe, so `unwrap_or_abort` is worse than `unsafe { unwrap_unchecked }`.

> I just confirmed RUST_BACKTRACE will produce backtrace just fine.

Well in simple situations, sure. But do you mean in a double panic situation, in liballoc code as compiled by x.py with optimize=false, debug=true, debug-assertions=true?

body:
> I want do be able to automatically exit the span on `Drop`. When I use `.enter()` I get a guard, but this guard borrows the `Span`, so I can't store both of them in the same datastructure.

Ah, okay, that makes sense. A change we could make upstream to better support this use case is adding a method to `Span` that's like `enter`, but takes the span by value, and returns an owned guard. The owned guard would have an explicit `exit` method that returns the unentered span, as well as exiting on drop. I discussed this proposal here: https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/issues/79#issuecomment-503276300

This would be quite simple to implement upstream. Thus far, we haven't done so just because there doesn't seem to be a whole lot of demand for it, but this seems like a good use-case.
author: hawkw

body: Another note: this type should probably not implement `Send`. Entering a span applies to the _current_ thread; when a span is entered, the thread on which `enter` is called is considered to be in that span. While the `Span` type can be freely sent or shared across threads, the entry should not — if this type is sent to a different thread and then dropped, it will call `exit` on _that_ thread, which may have never entered the span; meanwhile, the thread where the span _was_ entered will remain in that span forever.

I suggested documenting the order because if it's `FnMut`, it's likely that people will start to depend on it, and when it's not documented there are often follow-up PRs requesting that it get documented anyway (for example, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/60396 for `retain`).

body:
From `core::ptr#Safety`:

> For a pointer to be valid, it is necessary, but not always sufficient, that the pointer be dereferenceable: the memory range of the given size starting at the pointer must all be within the bounds of a single allocated object.

The safety constraint from `AllocRef` requires this:
> Memory blocks returned from an allocator must point to valid memory.

We have to elaborate on this in the allocator-wg, but this is another topic. Basically it is required for all allocators, that a valid pointer is returned. For this, there are currently two issues open: https://github.com/rust-lang/wg-allocators/issues/65 https://github.com/rust-lang/wg-allocators/issues/46. The former wants to refine the quoted phrase from `AllocRef`.

To sum up: This is not initialized, but valid. As long as we don't return `&[T]` this should be fine.
author: TimDiekmann

body: That is *valid for a given access kind and size*. But what your text here says sounds more like "valid for a given type", which -- for me at least -- is something [very different](https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2018/08/22/two-kinds-of-invariants.html).
author: RalfJung

body:
I don't think I quite follow. Which validity invariant am I missing here?

The whole reason to use an allocator (and let's assume that `Global` is implemented correctly here) is to get back a memory region that we can write to. Such a memory area may contain anything, uninitialized, but has a fixed size of at least `NonNull::len()`. For me this is just like returning a slice of `MaybeUninit<u8>` with a size of `len()`. Since `alloc` returns `NonNull<[u8]>`, it is guaranteed that no padding exists between `ptr[0]` and `ptr[1]` as [`u8` has no padding bits and its size is exactly one byte](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/layout/scalars.html#fixed-width-integer-types). So why is `&[MaybeUninit<u8>]` not a valid representation?

It may well be that I overlook or misunderstand something, but at the moment I cannot see the reason.

> Which validity invariant am I missing here?

`u8` must be initialized. So allocators do not return valid `u8`.

Your safety docs get it (almost) right, it says

> The pointer must be valid for reads (and writes) for `ptr.len() * mem::size_of::<T>()` many bytes

So the code's safety comment should match those docs. But it does not.
The correct thing to say would be something like "`memory` is valid for reads and writes for `memory.len()` many bytes".

> So why is &[MaybeUninit<u8>] not a valid representation?

I never said that. The code is fine. Just the comment justifying the code is not. I guess I wasn't clear enough about that, sorry for the confusion.

[EOPNOTSUPP shouldn't be visible to userspace](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/64bf5ff58dff757253cf2142542672de4b21cd1a#diff-63018726069897e4a3a3b5b03ff71613R1673), the kernel will (should) fallback to a generic splice in that case.

body:
The O(n^2) is not true (¹): the capacity doubling performs in O(n), making each push amortized O(1). See [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_array#Geometric_expansion_and_amortized_cost). `with_capacity` actually doesn't change anything about the asymptotic runtime, "just" about the constants.

(¹) It is technically true, as O(...) is just an upper bound, so O(n!) is also true. But most people use O(...) to mean Θ(...) so it is expected to specify the lowest possible upper bound in O(...).

This can very well be an additional function, but I think it should factor into the API design.

As [I argued in your previous PR](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/74178#issuecomment-659703970), I would prefer seeing an RFC for this API. There has been a lot of "prior art" (both, in external crates and other languages), and the design space is quite large. I think a proper summary would aid discussion a lot. People in the last PR rather disagreed with that, saying that an RFC would be overkill. 

The forge currently says:

> New unstable features don't need an RFC before they can be merged. If the feature is small, and the design space is straightforward, stabilizing it usually only requires the feature to go through FCP. Sometimes however, you may ask for an RFC before stabilizing.

I don't think "the design space is straightforward", which would imply an FCP is not sufficient for stabilization. We can of course merge it already since it's unstable anyway, but I don't really see the point of that if the API might very well be completely changed.

body:
> What does self profiling need the `WithOptConstParam` for?

Some queries (e.g. `mir_build`) take `WithOptConstParam` values as keys. Since self-profiling can record a string representation for each query key that gets used some of those keys will be stringified `WithOptConstParam` values. You can find the full list of queries (and their keys) in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/src/librustc_middle/query/mod.rs.

> You probably want to uniquely identify query calls? Considering that `self.const_param_did` should be unique for each `DefId` (as we otherwise cause an ICE while building mir) you might also be able to store this as `(did, bool)` for some additional wins.

I'm not quite sure I follow. You are saying that there is an invariant around `const_param_did` that makes sure that it is always the same (or `None`) for a given `did` value? 

In any case, I think it's a good idea to keep this as close to the original value as possible. The encoding format should make sure that there is no data redundancy (assuming that that DefId was already mentioned somewhere already).

Yes, that `AllocId` is dangling, but there's nothing with that `AllocId` anymore unless the caller of `intern_with_temp_alloc` copies it out of the `f` closure while it's being run. Note that it's dangling even before the `InterpCx` and `Memory` are dropped, as the `self.memory.alloc_map.remove` takes it out of there without even inserting anything into the `dead_alloc` table. This means any mis-use will give you an ICE.

What this function returns is a `&'tcx Allocation`, which doesn't need an `AllocId` that points to it. If a user of `intern_with_temp_alloc` wants an `AllocId` for the Allocation, they can invoke https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/ty/struct.TyCtxt.html#method.create_memory_alloc which will give them a new `AllocId`

Thanks for the callout. Good question.

The referenced line of code is a great place for me to re-insert the FIXME comment I had removed from rustc:mir::interpret::intrinsics. I just [pushed a change adding some comments here, for `step`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75563/files#diff-fabaa9592cbf2a32d5acb6e8cc047908).

Correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe it is reasonable to treat the Coverage statement as a NOP, if evaluated in a const expression, at this time. The statement is injected by a MIR pass, in a way that should not have any side effects on the runtime behavior, so ignoring it here effectively "un-injects" it, as if it never existed (right?).

If the Coverage statement is a "Counter" kind, it would normally result in LLVM-generated runtime code of only three statements: load a global int, increment it, and store it. 

If and/or what we might want to do in the future is the subject of the FIXME issue #73156.

body:
> Correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe it is reasonable to treat the Coverage statement as a NOP, if evaluated in a const expression, at this time. The statement is injected by a MIR pass, in a way that should not have any side effects on the runtime behavior, so ignoring it here effectively "un-injects" it, as if it never existed (right?).

Yes, that sounds right.

Note that your comment only seems to take into account CTFE. This code here is also used by [the Miri UB checker](https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/). So it has to adequately model all UB. But since coverage does not exist on the source level, and since presumably it is not something the program can interact with directly, I assume there also is no UB to check for here.

The comment should be adjusted taking into account that this is not just used for const expressions. The Miri engine is a general-purpose MIR interpreter, const evaluation is just one of its users.

The dereferenecability requirement could (I think) be encoded by having `Deref` as a super-trait, and you could use `<Self as Deref>::Target` instead of `Pointee`. body:
An `iter::from_fn` function is _almost always_ going to be inherently stateful, and iterators don't inherently have indices and a length. On the other hand, an array _does_ have indices and is constructed with a specified finite length — and this means that there is usually some significance to the index of an element, which is frequently useful for computing the element based on its position. Requiring setting up a mutable variable will clutter those common use cases.

If `T::from_fn(F)` functions are to be considered a pattern, then `F`'s parameters should be chosen to reflect the nature of `T`, not just to be similar to each other. Iterators mutate themselves, so the function mutates itself; arrays can be randomly accessed, so the function will often care about which index it's computing more than state carried from the preceding element.

body:
A few thoughts on this:

- I don't particularly like adding `IteratorExt`. It's an extra trait in the API that needs to be imported (as we can't easily add traits to the prelude). And for most users (using `std`), the split doesn't make sense. Maybe this should just be a function? 

- The `Join` trait is still unstable, meaning we could still change it (as long as we keep the current impls). And we can certainly implement it for new types. With that, it should be possible to avoid the `collect` into a `Vec`, right? I mean, ideally we only want the target "collection" (e.g. String) to allocate, as mentioned in the chat.

- `Iterator[Ext]::join` might not be a great name. `Iterator` uses lots of names from the functional programming/Haskell world (`last`, `map`, `fold`, `any`, `all`, `scan`, `take_while`, ...). And there, `join` already has a pretty established meaning that is very different from what this function does. 

- I think `intersperse` (returning a lazy iterator) is a useful method to have. However, I see that's kind of problematic to replace the `join` suggested here. If the separator is a string, not a single char, then the separator would need to be cloned a bunch of times which is likely not very fast. One might come up with a solution involving `Cow` (and `String` can be collected from an iterator over `Cow<str>`), but that's also not that nice of an API?
